Anyone with that trunk history can then fetch the branch using the same pack.
Several of these improvements are already in upstream Git, and many others in our public repository. We’re continuing to work with the Git community to make these improvements useful beyond Pando. You can follow that work in our public patch tracker(opens in a new window).
By rethinking conventional wisdom on how to scale Git repositories, Pando enables us to scale our monorepo without changing the Git workflows our engineers and agents already use. In our monorepo, Pando has unlocked a greater degree of parallelism, improved merge reliability, and reduced the time it takes to publish code changes. Beyond our monorepo, we’re also exploring other uses for Pando within OpenAI, including workloads where large numbers of agents need to collaborate on a shared Git repository.
As engineers and agents produce more software, more teams beyond OpenAI will encounter the limits we hit in source control. We’re currently exploring ways to share the technology that makes Pando possible with our users.
Pando builds on two decades of experience from users and operators of Git repositories. We’ll continue to develop Pando while working with the open-source Git community to share any improvements that benefit Git users more broadly.

articles.title: Scaling Git at OpenAI
articles.body:
Scaling Git at OpenAI
Building agentic-scale source control while investing in the Git ecosystem.
Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible.
We built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth.
We met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.
Here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.
Codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI.
These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit.
Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.
We saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from our copy of Git(opens in a new window) to upstream, sharing them with the broader community.
Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both.
First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time.
Second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation.
These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history.
Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync: objects and references.
A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository.
Objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a new blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects.
Branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a new commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it.
Git stores objects in either a “loose” or “packed” state. Loose objects are stored in individual files identified by their object ID. Packed objects are stored together in a packfile, enabling similar objects to be stored as deltas against one another.
In Git, an object is reachable from a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned.
A push transfers objects in the other direction by asking the server to update one or more refs. The client uses the server’s set of advertised refs to avoid sending objects the server already has. The pack being sent can therefore depend on existing objects: receiving the pack alone is not enough to reconstruct the new history.
Replicating a Git repository means keeping both objects and references available across multiple servers. Before a replica can serve a reference’s new value, it must be able to supply the objects reachable from that value. The service also needs to coordinate competing reference updates, i.e., pushes that try to move the same branch from the same old tip to different new commits. Systems that impose a single order on all writes to a repository can make pushes to unrelated branches wait on one another.
While designing Pando, we evaluated conventional approaches for scaling source control using Git: one that coordinates ref updates across repository replicas using three-phase commit (3PC, a protocol for coordinating a commit across multiple nodes), and one that orders updates through a shared write-ahead log (WAL, a record of changes written before they’re applied) in blob storage.
In the three-phase commit design we modeled, the Git service keeps a complete copy of the repository on several replicas. When any server receives a push, the incoming packfile is copied and sent to all replicas in parallel. To publish the push, a majority of replicas must accept the ref update. The server managing this is the coordinator, and it requires multiple rounds of communication between the coordinator and each other replica.
To accept a reference update, each replica locks its copy of the ref and checks that it still points to the commit the client expects. The coordinator then sends a pre-commit message to the replicas that accept. Once a majority acknowledges the pre-commit message, the coordinator tells them to perform the update. Any up-to-date replica can then advertise the new branch tip from its local copy of the repository.
Keeping complete replicas makes it possible to serve reads locally, and guarantees that clients get a consistent view of all references no matter which replica they pick. As a consequence, references are updated one at a time, and each push requires multiple round trips to coordinate the ref update among replicas.
Waiting for a quorum puts replica disk performance and communication latency on the push path. As write volume grows, the replicas must keep up with incoming packs as well as read traffic.

Writers can upload their packfiles in parallel, but even pushes to unrelated branches require updating the same manifest. The blob store can receive packfiles in parallel, but updates to the shared manifest still compete with one another. Increasing the blob store’s capacity alone doesn’t resolve that bottleneck. Each replica still needs to read and index packs from the blob store before it can serve them locally. However, an under-appreciated feature of the Git protocol, packfile-uri, allows a server to return links to download additional packs separately. Pando uses this exclusively, and transmits an empty packfile inline. To support this feature, OpenAI contributed a number of improvements to packfile-uri upstream.
OpenAI systems operate in many geographic regions, so we maintain Pando clusters with local caches in each. A pack delivery service, Express, caches our blob store, and a separate service caches the metadata store. These caches enable Pando to serve requests for a commit ID or a special read of a ref entirely from the cached state in that cluster. We use consistent hashing to route requests for a packfile to Express servers, with cache hit rates of over 99%.
This system of caches provides extremely high throughput, capable of saturating the network limit between clients and Pando. Using these packfile URIs and local caches, we’ve validated that using only standard cloud provider virtual machines, we see clone and fetch operations saturate 10 Gbps network links.
For most Git servers, repacking and garbage collection are necessary to maintain the performance of a growing repository. Both of these steps reclaim space, but are compute- and I/O-intensive.
In a fast-moving repository like OpenAI’s monorepo, it is infeasible to send an individual packfile URI for every push that has occurred since the last fetch. Each day, a client would need to download tens of thousands of packfiles to catch up their trunk.
Instead, Pando combines packs in the background to reduce this overhead, adopting a design similar to compaction in log-structured merge-trees. Each push produces what Pando refers to as an “L0” packfile, representing the smallest unit of data Pando can transmit. Over time, background workers collect these packfiles into covers spanning a sequence of ref versions, scaling geometrically from L0. Today, our monorepo uses up to L4 packfile covers.
These covers serve a dual purpose. After a cover is sufficiently full, a compaction worker will claim it and produce a single packfile. This improves the compression ratio by reorganizing the objects inside the packfile. But it also improves fetch negotiation performance by acting as skip list over ref versions. By scanning through indexes at each level simultaneously, Pando can select a set of packs to send to a client in logarithmic time. These packfile covers, repacked or not, enable a more efficient solution to fetch planning, reducing both throughput and latency requirements for Pando.
Compaction in Pando
Small packfiles are grouped into larger covers across levels, improving compression and speeding up fetches.
Unlike many Git servers, packfiles are kept at every level and not discarded or garbage collected. Packs at every level are used to serve clients continuously, based on the haves and wants they request in a fetch. And for clients using Pando as an API, reading an arbitrary object from a packfile tends to require reading less data from an L0 than an L4, because it’s less likely to be compressed.
Compaction in Pando significantly reduces both the total transfer size sent to clients and enables pack planning to scale sub-linearly in how far behind the client is. This is especially important for large and quickly changing repositories, which we expect to be a new normal in software development.
We built Pando with Codex, moving from kick-off to production, in just 10 weeks. The core of Pando was designed by a single engineer, implemented by teams of agents, and deployed by a handful of engineers. Pando began serving production traffic in April of this year, and is one part of a larger system of source control management tools used at OpenAI.
We employed a wide variety of approaches when validating Pando’s design. We applied our principles for building more secure software foundations. As a greenfield project, we chose to implement Pando in Rust and without legacy dependencies. We wrote a conformance test suite so agents could test their changes against standard Git behavior. We also developed deterministic simulation testing harnesses allowing us to check invariants and properties of the system, enabling us to find and mitigate subtle race conditions and regressions in negotiation and pack planning.
Many models contributed to this system; as new models became available, we used them to improve Pando’s performance and reliability. Using GPT‑6 Astra, agents wrote Lean and TLA+ to formalize a “theory of Pando” that we used to find and fix bugs in the implementation, and prove properties of the system. Multiple continuous sessions ran for hundreds of hours finding and fixing edge cases in Pando. We also run agents around the clock to red-team Git and Pando using Daybreak-capable models.
Our initial deployment of Pando was as a read- and write-through proxy to our existing source control system. This allowed us to keep Pando and the previous system in sync, so we could safely move traffic onto Pando without downtime.
As part of its caching design, Pando can also deduplicate and combine requests before proxying. This allowed us to keep our existing tools healthy as we moved systems to Pando one at a time. As we migrated more workloads to Pando, their pushes populated Pando’s cache and improved the reliability of our previous backend.
In order to optimize performance when using Pando, we began shipping our public distribution of Git to developer machines and within the ChatGPT desktop app. To migrate clients to Pando, we used an internal wrapper around the Git CLI to migrate clients in phases. We created many other tools for handling change requests, code review, and APIs for automations. We migrated hundreds of integrations that depended on legacy APIs, webhooks, and repository downloads alongside Git traffic.
Codex itself helped developers and teams make the move. We created skills for preparing existing checkouts, and for guiding agents to use the new system. As a result, developers could simply ask Codex to migrate their development environments and services.
Switching to Pando improved merge reliability and reduced the latency of the median push by nearly 80%.
Pando can deliver a petabyte of Git data per day with just a handful of CPU cores. Pando has served more than 57 terabytes of Git packs in a single hour, with more than 99% of those bytes from local disk cache.
Reusing packs lets many clients download the same repository history with little computation on the serving nodes. This example shows a single repository, but Pando is designed to support many more. As demand grows, we can scale data delivery and Git negotiation independently.
Building Pando on the Git protocol and client helped us identify bugs and opportunities to improve Git’s own performance.
For example, Pando serves reusable packs directly to clients, so downloading and indexing those packs became a central part of making the system fast and reliable. That work surfaced edge cases in concurrent downloads, cleanup after interrupted transfers, and resuming downloads that had already completed. We fixed those paths, added validations when accepting an existing pack for a fetch, and contributed that work back upstream.
We also needed to see where time and bandwidth were going, so we added tracing for packfile-uri downloads and byte counts for pack generation, making it easier to tell whether a slow fetch was spending its time generating packs or transferring them.
In OpenAI’s Git build(opens in a new window), the client can download and index independent packs in parallel. We added the concept of “explicit haves” so a server can advertise a branch’s current tip separately from the history a pushing client may leave out of its pack. On Pando, this enables clients to use --force-with-lease to check that a feature branch hasn’t moved and build its pack against trunk alone. Anyone with that trunk history can then fetch the branch using the same pack.
Several of these improvements are already in upstream Git, and many others in our public repository. We’re continuing to work with the Git community to make these improvements useful beyond Pando. You can follow that work in our public patch tracker(opens in a new window).
By rethinking conventional wisdom on how to scale Git repositories, Pando enables us to scale our monorepo without changing the Git workflows our engineers and agents already use. In our monorepo, Pando has unlocked a greater degree of parallelism, improved merge reliability, and reduced the time it takes to publish code changes. Beyond our monorepo, we’re also exploring other uses for Pando within OpenAI, including workloads where large numbers of agents need to collaborate on a shared Git repository.
As engineers and agents produce more software, more teams beyond OpenAI will encounter the limits we hit in source control. We’re currently exploring ways to share the technology that makes Pando possible with our users.
Pando builds on two decades of experience from users and operators of Git repositories. We’ll continue to develop Pando while working with the open-source Git community to share any improvements that benefit Git users more broadly.

articles.title: Midterm elections 2026: all the news
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm elections will determine the scope of President Donald Trump’s power in his final two years in office, and signal what voters care about going into the 2028 presidential election. While this year’s races are expected to be most broadly defined by affordability issues, there are several topics impacting the tech industry that appear to be on voters’ minds.
Among them are concerns about data centers, and whether voters will have to bear the burden of higher energy costs, AI safety, and the rapid expansion of surveillance technology through Flock. There’s also the question of how to tax billionaires’ wealth in California, a topic that has driven heavy tech spending and creative stock class structures meant to keep tech executives from fleeing the state should a ballot measure pass.
The next Congress is likely to continue grappling with how to regulate AI, and stem the data center backlash, among other issues. How that conversation shapes up, and which tech CEOs are hauled to testify on Capitol Hill, will be shaped by the outcome of November 3rd.
- This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump It’s the midterms! Here’s a fun fact for you as you head to the polls: Gas prices today are the highest ever recorded for a US Election Day. The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.12 and $6.28 for a gallon of diesel, according to GasBuddy. Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is maintained by the US Department of Energy as a safeguard during energy crises, is down to 282.2 million barrels of crude, the lowest level in 44 years. Read Article >
- Severe weather is affecting some voters across the country. In Florida, more than 20 polling sites are being moved due to intense flooding. Storms in the Southwest have also impacted some polling locations in Colorado, Newsweek reports, while Utah will let some voters impacted by flooding return ballots electronically, and Arizona officials are warning voters to check travel updates.
- A ballot scanner issue is impacting a New York suburb. Polling sites across Westchester County are experiencing an issue with their voting machines, but officials say residents can still safely cast their ballots. Election officials have a backup protocol in place to ensure voting can continue. Voting Machine Snags Are Reported in New York Suburbs [New York Times]
- Election protection hotline has received 3,000 calls this morning. The nonpartisan coalition running the 866-OUR-VOTE hotline says the calls range from asking about general information, to reporting long lines, lack of signage, or voting equipment issues. Texas, Michigan, Ohio, Pennsylvania, and New York account for the most calls. So far, no calls about federal agents at the polls.
- DOJ sends 1,000 election monitors to watch polls in every state. Federal election monitors are a standard procedure, but this year the Trump administration has expanded it to the “largest monitoring effort in history.” States have prepared to make sure they don’t interfere, as the administration has taken several steps this year to assert more oversight of state-run elections.
- Prop 45 in California could be hiding a loophole for data centers A high-stakes California ballot measure pitched as a fast track for “essential” infrastructure could wind up giving data center developers a loophole to evade public scrutiny, environmental advocates warn. Proposition 45 would shorten timelines for state-mandated environmental assessments for eligible projects and make it more difficult for residents to challenge those projects in court. Proponents say passing the measure would help alleviate the state’s housing shortage and meet rising electricity demand with new renewable energy projects. Environmental groups and some legal experts, however, warn that data center developers backing the proposition could escape scrutiny if Prop 45 becomes law. Read Article >
- Another election year, another tech company war room. OpenAI is the latest tech company (and according to Politico, the first major AI company) to set up a command center for fighting election misinfo and abuse of its systems, approaching the second major AI-era US election: The Election Operations Center will begin running this week until all votes are counted, to identify the potential spread of misinformation or other efforts to disrupt the elections. It’s meant in large part to combat abuse of the company’s own tools like ChatGPT, monitoring real-time events and fielding reports of unexpected behavior from models or cases of suspected violations of their platform’s terms.
- Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers Ask Texas NAACP president Gary Bledsoe what it’s been like to see data center developers descend upon Austin and its surrounding suburbs and he can rattle off project after project facing opposition from locals. There’s the fight in Taylor over plans to build a data center at a site that’s supposed to be a park. Temple, around 40 miles away, is another sore spot, Bledsoe says. The mayor and City Council members there face recall attempts over data center developments. And some 30 miles outside of Austin, San Marcos became the first city in all of Texas to ban data centers. Read Article >
- Data center backlash is uniting America If there’s one issue that seems to activate all kinds of voters in 2026, it’s data centers. The rapid buildout of these massive server storage facilities — and the infrastructure construction and expenses that come with them — has sparked local opposition in communities across the country and become a major issue in many congressional and gubernatorial campaigns. At the same time, tech money has been pouring into many of these races. Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and OpenAI President Greg Brockman, has already spent $45 million in a year. And Public First Action, an Anthropic-backed group that says it supports AI safeguards, says it’s raised $80 million. Both have funded Democratic and Republican-aligned groups. Other super PACs see an opportunity to push for stricter AI policies, like the recently created Tomorrow Together, which launched $4 million in ads for battleground House races, with messages about data center development and AI safety. Read Article >
- Republican politicians have embraced anti-Indian racism — and it’s costing them votes Two years ago, University of Houston student Vasant Bhatt was doing everything he could to help Republicans regain power. He knocked doors for Sen. Ted Cruz’s reelection campaign and helped organize his community for Donald Trump, two victories he, like many other Republicans, celebrated in 2024. But this week, Bhatt did something unexpected: He voted for Texas Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico, and he publicly urged others to do the same. Bhatt, whose father is a small-business owner, tells The Verge he was initially drawn to the Republican Party due to its economic principles. “The strong belief in individual liberty and limited government,” he says, led him to identify as a conservative. More recently, however, another aspect of his family’s experience has driven him away from the party. As an Indian American, Bhatt feels increasingly unwelcome in a party where racist rhetoric is becoming far too common. Read Article >
- Meta made a deal to keep Mark Zuckerberg from leaving California over its billionaire tax. It said in a filing that Zuckerberg “was evaluating relocating his primary residence” if California’s Proposition 40 passes. As Bloomberg reports, Meta’s board issued special shares so that he wouldn’t have to leave: Zuckerberg gets non-voting shares he can sell for liquidity without reducing his voting control. In return, he has committed to remain in California — or wherever Meta is headquartered — for eight years while he remains in a full-time leadership role.
- Trump is giving Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million fraud bounty program Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance said on Tuesday that the Trump administration was giving right-wing YouTuber Nick Shirley $10,000 and launching a $25 million bounty program for members of the public to report fraud. In December 2025, Shirley published a viral video alleging fraud at daycares in Minnesota that were operated by members of the local Somali community. Shirley lingered in parking lots and asked to enter childcare centers, taking refusals as evidence that the centers weren’t actually caring for children. The video quickly went viral, triggering a massive governmental response: Federal immigration agents descended on the Minneapolis area, and the Trump administration froze Minnesota’s federal funding for childcare. Shirley has since visited other states in the US under similar pretenses, showing up unannounced to grocery stores and hospice centers in search of evidence of fraud. Vance and others in the administration publicly praised Shirley, who has since become a mainstay in the MAGA-aligned content creator ecosystem. He’s helped popularize a genre of so-called independent journalism popular on the right in which content creators and influencers confront businesses or people they suspect of fraud or crime as the basis for their online content. Harassment — or even immigration crackdowns — often follow. Read Article >
- Democrats think cracking down on AI could give them an edge Democrats could win back control of Congress this November, and if they do, they’ll need to decide how to approach one of the country’s newest and thorniest political issues: AI. Polls predict Democrats will flip at least one chamber of Congress in the midterm elections, which would put committee leadership back in their hands. That could usher in a wave of newfound scrutiny for AI companies. Top Democrats on key committees have already signaled their willingness to press the industry on tax credits tied to data centers and recent hacking incidents, and would be able to set committee agendas if they take over, allowing them to call CEOs to testify in Congress and demand documents that explain companies’ inner workings. Read Article >
- Tech billionaires have reportedly donated over $340 million to fight a wealth tax in California. According to The Guardian, the campaign they’re funding is spending over $1 million per day trying to defeat Proposition 40, which would enact a one-time 5 percent tax on California’s billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly the biggest donor, contributing at least $102 million, alongside other tech executives: The donors to the no campaign are a who’s who of Silicon Valley, including the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, crypto magnate Chris Larsen and several prominent venture capitalists.
- Elon Musk has donated over $276 million to Republican midterm efforts Elon Musk has handed out at least $276 million to Republican groups since July, The New York Times reports, making him both the party’s top known donor and the biggest established midterm donor. $158 million of that money — one of the largest political donations in American history — has been funneled into the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC that aims to secure and maintain a Republican Senate majority. Among others, it’s fighting to retain the party’s Senate seat in Texas, which serves as a major hub for Musk’s business empire. He’s also donated over $76 million to America PAC, a super PAC Musk founded in 2024 that canvasses for hard-to-reach Republican voters. Smaller amounts have also been given to other conservative groups, including: Read Article >
- The midterms are going to be a data security nightmare One messy database is threatening to disenfranchise thousands or even millions of registered voters, while leaving even more at risk of intimidation or data breaches, in the name of solving a problem that barely exists. As the 2026 midterm elections approach, election and privacy experts are sounding alarms about the Department of Homeland Security’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements (SAVE) Program, which President Donald Trump’s administration has expanded to ostensibly catch noncitizens voting. Experts say that amounts to a dangerous, error-prone effort to centralize voter data. “The federal government doesn’t have the authority to do any of that and doesn’t have the expertise either,” says Eileen O’Connor, senior counsel at the Brennan Center. “Inserting themselves into the day-to-day functioning of state elections is unprecedented and disturbing.” Read Article >
- Democrats preview how they’d go after the Ticketmaster settlement if they regain power A handful of Democrats called an unofficial hearing on Capitol Hill Monday to slam the Department of Justice’s “trivial” and “pathetic” settlement with Live Nation-Ticketmaster, previewing how they might go after Trump administration antitrust deals if they win back congressional power in November. While the DOJ settlement with Live Nation, which came one week into trial and with a promise of up to $280 million, received copious pushback, Democrats don’t at the moment have the power in either chamber to set committee agendas. That meant that Monday’s so-called shadow hearing looked different than most official proceedings. Instead of sitting at the elevated seats behind the dais, the lawmakers sat at tables below, eye level with witnesses including California Attorney General Rob Bonta, one of the AGs continuing the fight against Live Nation-Ticketmaster, ousted Trump administration antitrust official Roger Alford, and several entertainment industry players, including a member of the band The Hold Steady. Several artists asked to appear at the forum declined out of fear for their livelihoods, according to House Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Jamie Raskin (D-MD), who co-hosted the forum with Senate Homeland Security permanent subcommittee on investigations Ranking Member Richard Blumenthal (D-CT). Read Article >
- AI backlash is coming for elections Ask Americans how they feel about AI and most say they have concerns. Communities have mounted resistance to data center projects, stalling them across the US. On social media, anger at AI companies and executives is unrestrained — sometimes to the point of condoning violence. But look at the issues that most campaigns are focused on, and AI is far less prevalent, experts say. Read Article >

articles.title: CrowdStrike to shell out nearly $500M for 2 AI security startups as the market for securing agents takes off
articles.body:
Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike is buying two AI security companies that expand its products to more broadly monitor, test, and cover AI models and agents, as companies across industries start rolling out AI agents and models wholesale.
CrowdStrike said it will buy Fiddler AI, which makes observability software for monitoring AI agents inside enterprises, and Dreadnode, which helps companies automate security testing specifically aimed at detecting flaws in AI models, apps, and agents before they are set live.
The company is paying around $400 million for Fiddler AI, and about $95 million for Dreadnode, according to The Wall Street Journal.
The deals are happening at a time of significant upheaval in the cybersecurity space, especially as companies’ policies and processes lag behind AI adoption within their walls. Teams and individual employees alike are experimenting with AI tools, automating workflows, vibe-coding custom apps, and deploying armies of AI agents to do their bidding, which is understandably causing headaches for security teams.
CrowdStrike, whose products are used widely across enterprises and governments, is clearly trying to leverage its already significant heft and presence to capture a share of this quickly burgeoning market. It’s not alone, of course, as we’ve already seen several startups and cybersecurity vendors raising dozens of millions in funding to solve issues for companies, though most of these approaches are essentially based on the conviction that existing security software isn’t enough to monitor and control AI tools, connectors, or usage.
The company has itself been building detection and response controls, dubbed Falcon Guardian, to help companies see and understand what agents are doing on their devices, and these acquisitions seem to further flesh out its offerings.
Fiddler AI is going to be part of CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform as Falcon Observe, where it’ll ostensibly help the company’s clients evaluate agents before they’re deployed, understand their actions, and monitor what they do, and feed that information as telemetry into the broader platform. Dreadnode, meanwhile, will be integrated into the Falcon Guardian product, to which the startup’s software will feed its testing results as security policy recommendations.
Founded in 2018, Fiddler AI has raised a total of about $99 million to date, according to PitchBook. Dreadnode, founded in 2023, has raised $14 million so far.

articles.title: Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
articles.body:
Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is rolling out into beta testing on Tuesday, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
The news was first announced via an emailed press release sent out by Apple’s communications team in India early on Tuesday. The update rolled out in the U.S. and other markets later in the day.
The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.
However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.
Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.
With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the stand-alone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.
Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.
When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.
These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.
The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.
Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.
Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.
This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.
At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.
This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning.
Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.
Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.
The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.
The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.
To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately afterwards.)
The recaps you can then access on your iPhone are only accessible to you, not to Apple. And they’re encrypted when they’re synced between your multiple Apple devices.
Similarly, Apple Watch transfers audio to the iPhone for processing to create the 15-second snippets for Live Rewind.
Apple says none of these features should impact the battery life of your watch or phone. The features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.
Post updated after publication to indicate the current status of the software’s rollout.

articles.title: Y Combinator’s Garry Tan uses AI agents so much, he spends up to $200K a year on tokens
articles.body:
Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan has, in the past, jokingly admitted that he’s suffered from “cyber psychosis” and sometimes barely sleeps because he’s so excited to be working with his AI agents. On a new episode of Walter Isaacson’s podcast The Builders, set to publish on Tuesday, Tan put a price tag on his passion.
“I spend about maybe $100[,000] to $200,000 a year on tokens,” he told Isaacson. He uses agents for countless work projects and coding tasks and has freely shared his set of 23 Claude Code skills, called gstack, on GitHub — an effort to help teach others what agents can do, he said.
On the one hand, he uses his agent the way many people use AI: to help him research Isaacson’s podcast and prep for the kinds of questions he might be asked. On the other, his agent also helps him run his life.
“It’s read all of my email and all of my Dropbox. It’s read, like, all of my Apple Notes, even my therapy notes going back 20 years,” he said.
He describes using AI agents as getting help with “almost anything that you do in your day-to-day life, and for it to do it somewhat more autonomously. Think of it as a Jiminy Cricket on your shoulder at all times. Like, almost anything you want to do, it knows you, and it’s there to help. And it will actually sort of run ahead and say, ‘What about this?’ Or it’ll help you see around corners.”
As an early OpenClaw adopter who is now a power user, Tan says one thing he’s learned is not to treat AI agents like traditional software. Some people are so worried about “repeatability and safety that they actually trade off all of the beautiful parts of working with an AI agent, which basically can be so similar to a human,” he said.
For instance, Y Combinator is also using an agent that is “rebuilding the way we operate at YC,” he said. “We now have an internal AI agent, for instance, named Stray Light that kind of has a personality, and then it has a company brain. Like it actually has the total context of every founder we’ve ever backed, anyone who’s ever emailed us, like all the applications.”
Tan, who is, naturally, an avid lover of technology (as anyone running Silicon Valley’s famed startup accelerator would be), believes personal AI agents will eventually become mainstream, if one major problem is solved: Costs have got to come down.
“It’s too expensive right now,” he said, adding that he knows the amount of money he spends on AI agents is “a crazy privilege that not everyone can do.”
But freebie agents controlled by Big Tech maybe aren’t the answer, either. When discussing the future he’d like tech to build, and how Meta as a social media company has impacted us, he said, “This is a huge company that controls the algorithm, and we all wish that they didn’t at some level,” he said. “So you could imagine a personal AI that you control, that you program.”

articles.title: SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
articles.body:
SLAC researchers find proof of altermagnetism, a new magnetic phase
The team directly observed a unique property in an altermagnetic candidate material, delivering key evidence of a new phase of magnetism first postulated in 2022.
Key takeaways:
- The scientific case for a third type of magnetism – termed “altermagnetism” – has been building over recent years.
- Now, a SLAC-led team has experimentally proven that a material exhibits characteristics that are theoretically impossible to explain without altermagnetism.
- Altermagnetic materials could be used to design advanced electronics, with applications including quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.
For decades, physicists recognized only two types of magnetism that occur in materials without external influence: ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Today, in findings published in Science, a team led by the U.S. Department of Energy's SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory has delivered conclusive experimental proof of a third magnetic phase called altermagnetism.
“In the past few years, scientists have observed phenomena that don't fit neatly into the ferromagnetism-antiferromagnetism dichotomy,” explained lead author Daniel Jost, associate scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences. “Researchers have been compiling evidence of a third type of magnetism that bridges the qualities of these two classes. We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase – altermagnetism – is real.”
Building on previous studies, this research confirmed that manganese telluride (MnTe) is an altermagnet – a new class of magnet that exhibits properties of both ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism. Their results showed direct experimental evidence of chirality – an asymmetric magnetic structure, akin to a spiral staircase or a screw – in the spins of an altermagnetic candidate material.
Identifying these unique materials could allow researchers to manipulate their properties in ways that make them ideal candidates for advanced electronics, with applications including quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.
A primer on magnetism
To most of us, magnetism is a tangible force: It’s what holds a child's artwork to a refrigerator door and points a compass needle north. But to a physicist, magnetism is more complex. It’s a quantum property of a material, and not all magnetic materials have a directly observable magnetic effect.
In physics, a material is considered magnetic if its electrons’ spins – their internal angular momentum, which can be either “up” or “down” – are polarized, or ordered in a specific pattern.
In ferromagnets, all electronic spins point the same direction (up-up-up or down-down-down), creating an observable magnetic field. Humans have known about and made use of this class of magnets since ancient times. In 1933, scientists discovered another type of material with polarized spins. Antiferromagnets have alternating electronic spins (up-down-up-down) that cancel each other out, producing no net magnetic effect.
A new type of magnetism?
For nearly 90 years, this two-category system dominated our understanding of magnetism.
But in recent years, researchers have noticed that some materials don’t fit neatly into either category. Certain materials seemed to exhibit features of both antiferromagnetism, such as alternating spin configuration with no net magnetization, and ferromagnetism, such as the ability to use spin currents. These behaviors were once thought to be mutually exclusive.
In 2022, researchers proposed the term “altermagnets” to label this wily class of materials.
    
    
We believe our results provide robust experimental confirmation that this third phase – altermagnetism – is real.
Associate Scientist at SLAC and Stanford Institute for Materials and Energy Sciences
To explain this behavior, researchers postulated that altermagnets exhibit an alternating spin polarization (up-down-up-down), much like conventional antiferromagnets, but with a crucial twist: the crystal lattice structure surrounding the “up” spins is rotated relative to the lattice surrounding the “down” spins. This geometric twist is a break in symmetry that could give rise to their unusual behavior.
Chirality: the final piece of the puzzle
“By 2024, there were some factors that spoke strongly in favor of altermagnetism being real,” Jost said, “but there was still a missing piece to the puzzle.”
That missing piece was experimental evidence of chirality in an altermagnetic candidate material. Chirality, often referred to as “handedness,” means a material cannot be superimposed on a mirror image of itself, just like a left hand cannot fit into a right-handed glove.
Chirality offers a clever way to distinguish subtle, quantum-level differences between antiferromagnets and suspected altermagnets: While an altermagnetic material would have alternating spins (up-down-up-down) like an antiferromagnet, the geometric twists in its lattice would give the material’s electronic and magnetic structure a distinct handedness that conventional antiferromagnets lack.
Jost’s team chose to investigate chirality in MnTe – a material considered antiferromagnetic for decades until a few years ago when it was suspected to be altermagnetic. The team brought it to the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility (ESRF) in France, to a beamline known for its ability to generate highly controlled polarized X-ray beams.
“Chiral materials scatter left-handed polarized X-ray beams differently than they do right-handed beams,” explained Jost. “Non-chiral materials would scatter each beam of light the same way.”
By scattering circularly polarized X-rays from the material and comparing how it responded to left- versus right-handed light, they teased out a clear chiral signal that shouldn’t exist in a conventional antiferromagnet.
“This chiral signature gave us the solid experimental ground to say altermagnetism stands in a class of its own,” Jost said. The initial experiment was completed in 2024; the team repeated their experiment in early 2025, confirming their earlier results.
“This technique helped us confirm that manganese telluride was really exhibiting altermagnetic properties,” said Rachel Nickel, postdoctoral scientist with ESRF, a co-author who helped design and conduct the experiment on the ID32 beamline. “Altermagnetism was only proposed a few years ago, and the rapid progress in confirming these models is incredible.”
Altermagnetism in the real world
This discovery has big implications for the field of spintronics, where researchers are leveraging the polarized spin of magnetic materials to design next-generation electronics.
Where traditional computing technologies use only an electron’s charge to store and move information, spintronics takes advantage of both an electron’s charge and its spin, giving researchers an additional control knob. Spintronic devices have the potential to be faster, be more robust and significantly decrease power consumption in computing and data centers.
Researchers have had some success with spintronic devices, but that success has been limited by the nature of ferro- and antiferromagnetism.
“Ferromagnets are too easily influenced by magnetic fields,” Jost explained. “If you have a permanent magnet in your pocket and walk by a spintronic device built with ferromagnets, you could start flipping the bits, scrambling the information stored there. Antiferromagnets fix that problem, but they are practically invisible – so you can’t easily read the data stored in them or use them to drive efficient spin currents.”
“Altermagnets combine the best of both,” Jost said. “They have zero net magnetization, so they're stable, but they still have the capability to generate spin-polarized currents needed to easily extract information. That gives you an additional degree of freedom to work with.”
Future research will explore how altermagnetic states can be influenced and controlled using light and electricity to enhance their usefulness in spintronic solutions for quantum technologies, memory devices and data centers.
This research is supported in part by the DOE Office of Science.
Citation: D. Jost et al., Science, 29 October 2026, 10.1126/science.adv3196.
For media inquiries, please contact media@slac.stanford.edu. For other questions or comments, contact SLAC Strategic Communications & External Affairs at communications@slac.stanford.edu.

SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory explores how the universe works at the biggest, smallest and fastest scales and invents powerful tools used by researchers around the globe. As world leaders in ultrafast science and bold explorers of the physics of the universe, we forge new ground in understanding our origins and building a healthier and more sustainable future. Our discovery and innovation help develop new materials and chemical processes and open unprecedented views of the cosmos and life’s most delicate machinery. Building on more than 60 years of visionary research, we help shape the future by advancing areas such as quantum technology, scientific computing and the development of next-generation accelerators.

articles.title: USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance
articles.body:
Computer Science > Databases
  [Submitted on 2 Nov 2026]
Title:USDB: Scaling Storage for Next-Generation Recommender Systems at ByteDance
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Recommendation models consume increasingly long, attribute-rich user histories, making small continuous updates and repeated large reads a central storage asymmetry. We present USDB, ByteDance's unified sequence storage practice for streaming and batch workloads. CascadeLSM time-based compaction stages materialize application-specific histories; differentiated replicas share persistent files; partial dumps reconstruct inference inputs from captured recent state and versioned history; and a hybrid columnar format accelerates projected reads. These designs reuse maintenance results across ingestion, inference, and training. Production migration records show 85.8% lower mean write latency, while normalized deployment accounting shows 42.1% lower infrastructure cost. Controlled comparisons with an Optimized RocksDB sequence baseline show faster long-history reads across projections and client loads. Aggregation pushdown sustains 8.5x the throughput of ordinary reads under a constrained receive budget. Production reconstruction and direct-file training results demonstrate how shared sequence maintenance supports fresh serving and repeated historical access.
