articles.title: Handles are the better pointers (2018)
articles.body:
Handles are the better pointers
28-Nov-2018: I’ve added a small update at the end on how to prevent ‘handle collisions’ with a per-slot generation counter
Original Post:
…wherein I talk a bit about how I’m doing dynamic memory management in C and C++ these days which basically replaces raw- and smart-pointers with ‘index-handles’.
In my last blog post I was mentioning pointer- and allocation-free programming, but was skipping over the details. This is what the following blog post is about.
This is all based on the (sometimes painful) experience of wrestling for 15+ years with fairly big C++ code bases (0.5 to around 1 mloc) where memory is often managed through smart pointers. The worst case being tens- to hundreds-of-thousands of small C++ objects, each in its own heap allocation, pointing to each other through smart pointers. While such code is quite robust in terms of memory corruption (segfaults and corruption rarely happens, since most attempts are caught by asserts when dereferencing smart pointers), this type of ‘object spiderweb code’ is also dog-slow without obvious starting points for optimization, since the entire code is full of cache misses. Other typical problems are memory fragmentation and ‘fake memory leaks’ because a forgotten smart pointer prevents freeing the underlying memory (I call them ‘fake leaks’ because this type of leaks cannot be caught by memory debugging tools).
Nothing presented here is particularly new or clever, it’s just a collection of a few simple ideas which together work fairly well in bigger code bases to prevent (or at least detect early) a number of common memory-related problems in C and C++, and may even be useful in higher-level garbage-collected languages to reduce pressure on the garbage collector.
However, the underlying design philosophy doesn’t fit very well into a classical OOP world where applications are built from small autonomous objects interacting with each other. That’s why it’s also quite tricky to implement those ideas in a big existing OOP code base, where object creation and destruction happens ‘decentralized’ all over the code.
The approach described here works very well though with a data-oriented architecture, where central systems work on arrays of data items packed tightly in memory.
Most of the following blog post is written from a game developer’s perspective, but should also apply to other areas where a program needs to juggle a few hundred to a few million objects (or generally ‘data items’) in memory, and where such items are created and destroyed frequently.
The gist is:
- move all memory management into centralized systems (like rendering, physics, animation, …), with the systems being the sole owner of their memory allocations
- group items of the same type into arrays, and treat the array base pointer as system-private
- when creating an item, only return an ‘index-handle’ to the outside world, not a pointer to the item
- in the index-handles, only use as many bits as needed for the array index, and use the remaining bits for additional memory safety checks
- only convert a handle to a pointer when absolutely needed, and don’t store the pointer anywhere
I’ll explain each of those points in detail below. But the idea is basically that common ‘user-level’ code doesn’t directly call memory allocation functions (like malloc, new or make_shared/make_unique), and reduces the use of pointers to an absolute minimum (only as short-lived references when direct memory access to an item is absolutely needed). Most importantly, pointers are never the ‘owner’ of an item’s underlying memory.
Instead, direct memory manipulation happens as much as possible inside a few centralized systems where memory-related problems are easier to debug and optimize.
Move memory management into central systems
In this blog post, a ‘system’ is a (usually fairly big) part of a code base which takes care of a number of related tasks, like ‘rendering’, ‘physics’, ‘AI’, ‘character animation’ and so on. Such a system is separated from other systems and ‘user-code’ through a clearly defined function API, and the work that happens on the system’s data is performed in tight central loops instead of being spread out all over the code base.
Systems often work on items created and destroyed under control of user code (but note that creation and destruction of items is different from allocating and freeing the memory used by those items!). For instance a rendering system might deal with vertex buffers, textures, shaders and pipeline state objects. A physics system works with rigid bodies, joints and collision primitives, and an animation system works with animation keys and curves.
It makes sense to move the memory management for such items into the systems themselves, because a general memory allocator doesn’t have the system-specific ‘domain knowledge’ about how data items are processed and the relationships between data items. This allows the system to optimize memory allocations, perform additional validation checks when creating and destroying items, and arrange items in memory for making best use of the CPU’s data caches.
A good example for this ‘system domain knowledge’ is the destruction of rendering resource objects with modern 3D APIs: a resource object can not simply be destroyed immediately when the user code says so because the resource might still be referenced in a command list waiting to be consumed by the GPU. Instead the rendering system would only mark the resource object for destruction when the user code requests its destruction, but the actual destruction happens at a later time when the GPU no longer uses the resource.
Group items of the same type into arrays
Once all memory management has moved into systems, the system can optimize memory allocations and memory layout with its additional knowledge about how items are used. One obvious optimization is to reduce the number of general memory allocations by grouping items of the same type into arrays, and allocate those arrays at system startup.
Instead of performing a memory allocation each time a new item is created, the system keeps track of free array slots, and picks the next free slot. When the user code no longer needs the item, the system simply marks the slot as free again instead of performing a deallocation (not different from a typical pool allocator).
This pool allocation is most likely a little bit faster than performing a memory allocation per item, but this is not even the main reason for keeping items in arrays (modern general allocators are quite fast too for small allocations).
A few additional advantages are:
- items are guaranteed to be packed tightly in memory, general allocators sometimes need to keep some housekeeping data next to the actual item memory
- it’s easier to keep ‘hot items’ in continuous memory ranges, so that the CPU can make better use of its data caches
- it’s also possible to split the data of a single item into several subitems in different arrays for even tighter packing and better data cache usage (AoS vs SoA and everything inbetween), and all those data layout details remain private to the system and are trivial to change without affecting ‘outside code’
- as long as the system doesn’t need to reallocate arrays, it is guaranteed that there will be no memory fragmentation (although this is less of an issue in a 64-bit address space)
- it’s easier to detect memory leaks early, and provide more useful error messages: when a new item is created a system can trivially check the current number of items against an expected upper bound (for instance a game might know that there should never be more than 1024 textures alive at a time, and since all textures are created through the rendering system, the system can print out a more useful warning message when this number is exceeded)
Public index-handles instead of pointers
Keeping system items in arrays instead of unique allocations has the advantage that an item can be identified through an array index instead of requiring a full pointer. This is very useful for memory safety. Instead of handing memory pointers to the outside world, the system can treat the array base pointers as ‘private knowledge’, and only hand out array indices to the public. Without the base pointer to compute an item’s memory location, the outside code can’t access the item’s memory, even with a lot of criminal energy.
This has a number of further advantages:
- In many situations, code outside the system never even needs to directly access memory of an item, only the system does. In such an ‘ideal’ situation, user code never accesses memory through pointers, and can never cause memory corruption.
- Since only the system knows the array base pointers, it’s free to move or reallocate the item arrays at will without invalidating existing index handles.
- Array indices need fewer bits than full pointers, and a smaller data type can be picked for them, which in turn allows tighter packing of data structures and better data cache usage (this has the caveat that additional handle bits can be used to increase memory safety, more about this below)
If user code needs to access the memory of an item directly it needs to obtain a pointer through a ‘lookup function’ which takes a handle as input and returns a pointer. As soon as such a lookup function exists, the fairly watertight memory safety scenario outlined above is no longer guaranteed, and the user code should adhere to a few rules:
- pointers should never be stored anywhere, since the next time the pointer is used it may no longer point to the same item, or even to valid memory
- a pointer should only be used in a simple code block, and not ‘across’ function calls
Every time a handle is converted into a pointer, the system can guarantee that the returned pointer still points to the same item that the handle was originally created for (more on this below), but this guarantee ‘decays’ over time since the item under the pointer may have been destroyed, or the underlying memory may have been reallocated to a different location (this is the same problem as iterator invalidation in C++).
The two simple rules above are easy to memorize and are a good compromise between not exposing pointers to user code at all, and having a (somewhat costly) handle-to-pointer conversion for every single memory access.
Memory safety considerations
First, each type of handle should get its own C/C++ type, so that attempting to pass the wrong handle type to a function is already detected at compile time (note that a simple typedef isn’t enough to produce a compiler warning, the handle must be wrapped into its own struct or class - however this could be limited to debug compilation mode).
All runtime memory safety checks happen in the function which converts a handle into a pointer. If the handle is just an array index, it would look like this:
- a range check happens for the index against the current item array size, this prevents segmentation faults and reading or writing allocated but unrelated memory areas
- a check needs to happen whether the indexed array item slot contains an active item (is not currently a ‘free slot’), this prevents the simple variant of ‘use after free’
- finally the item pointer is computed from the private array base pointer and public item index
The resulting pointer is safe to use as long as:
- the item array isn’t reallocated
- the indexed item hasn’t been destroyed
Both can only happen inside one of the system’s functions, that’s why the two ‘pointer usage rules’ exist (don’t store pointers, don’t keep pointers across function calls).
There is a pretty big hole in the above use-after-free check though: if we only check if an array slot behind an index-handle contains a valid item, it’s not guaranteed that it is the same item the handle was originally created for. It can happen that the original item was destroyed, and the same array slot was reused for a new item.
This is where the ‘free bits’ in a handle come in: Let’s say our handles are 16-bits, but we only ever need 1024 items alive at the same time. Only 10 index bits are needed to address 1024 items, which leaves 6 bits free for something else.
If those 6 bits contain some sort of ‘unique pattern’, it’s possible to detect dangling accesses:
- When an item is created, a free array item is picked and its index is put into the lower 10 handle bits. The upper 6 bits are set to a ‘unique bit pattern’
- The resulting 16-bit handle (10 bits index + 6 bit ‘unique pattern’) are returned to the outside world, and at the same time stored with the array slot.
- When an item is destroyed, the item handle stored with the array slot is set to the ‘invalid handle’ value (can be zero, as long as zero is never returned as a valid handle to the outside world)
- When the handle is converted to a pointer, the lower 10 bits are used as array index to lookup the array slot, and the entire 16-bit handle is compared against the handle that’s currently stored with the array slot:
    
  - if both handles are equal, the pointer is valid and points to the same item the handle was created for
  - otherwise this is a dangling access, the slot item has either been destroyed (in that case the stored handle would have the ‘invalid handle’ value), or has been destroyed and reused for a new item (in that case the upper 6 ‘unique pattern’ bits don’t match)
This handle-comparison check when converting a handle to a pointer works quite well to detect dangling-accesses, but it isn’t waterproof because the same combination of array index and ‘unique pattern’ will be created sooner or later. But it’s still better than no dangling protection at all (like raw pointers), or a ‘fake memory leak’ which would happen in similar situations with smart pointers.
Finding good strategies to create unique handles that collide as rarely as possible is the most important part of course, and left as an excercise to the reader ;P
Obviously it’s good to use as many bits for the unique pattern as possible, and the way how free array slots are reused is important as well (e.g. LIFO vs FIFO). It’s probably also good to write a little creation/destruction stress-test which checks for handle collisions and can be used to tweak the unique-pattern creation for specific use cases. A system where items are created and destroyed with a very high frequency needs more effort (or simply more handle bits) than systems where item creation and destruction is a rare occurance.
Other useful properties of handles
Apart from the whole memory safety aspect, handles are also useful for other situations where pointers are problematic:
Handles can be used as shared object identifiers across processes (all you need is some sort of ‘create_item_with_handle()’ function, which doesn’t create a new handle, but takes an existing handle as input argument). This is especially useful for online games where handles can be shared between the server and all clients in a game session, or in savegame systems to store references to other objects.
Sometimes it’s useful to create a whole group of related items (for instance animation keys and curves), and reference the whole item group with a single handle. In that case some sort of ‘range handle’ can be used, which contains not only an index (of the first item), but also the number of items in the range.
In some situations it’s also useful to reserve a few handle bits for an item type if static type checking at compile time isn’t sufficient.
In conclusion, I find it quite surprising how naturally and elegantly handles solve many problems I encountered in the past with the traditional ‘pointers to objects on the heap’ model, and how little I miss this model now (and the parts of C++ that are built around it).
Some real-world examples
The sokol-gfx API is an example of a C-API which uses handles instead of pointer of rendering resource objects (buffers, images, shaders, …):
The Oryol Gfx module is a similar 3D API wrapper, but written in C++:
The Oryol Animation extension module is a character animation system which keeps all its data in arrays:
Update 28-Nov-2018
…in the post above I was sort of handwaving away the problem of creating the same unique-tag twice for the same slot, and a nice person on twitter hinted me about a very simple, elegant and embarrassingly ‘obvious’ solution:
Each array slot gets its own generation counter, which is bumped when a handle is released (can also happen when the handle is created, but bumping on release means you don’t need a reserved value for “free slots” to detect an invalid handle).
To check if a handle is valid, simply compare its unique-tag with the current generation counter in its slot.
Once the generation counter would ‘overflow’, disable that array slot, so that no new handles are returned for this slot.
This is a perfect solution for avoiding handle collisions, but the handles will eventually run out since all array slots will be disabled eventually. But since each slot has its own counter, this only happens after all handle-bits are exhausted, not just the few unique-tag bits.
So with 32-bit handles, you can always create 4 billion items, with at most 2^(32 - num_counter_bits) alive at the same time. This also means the number of bits for the unique-tag can be reduced without compromising ‘handle safety’.
It may also be possible to re-activate disabled slots once it can be guaranteed that no more handles for that slot are out in the wild (maybe at special places in the code like entering or exiting a level).

articles.title: Mac at Any Scale
articles.body:
Mac at any scale
Chances are you’ve seen me on X: unpacking hundreds of MacBook Pros to deploy in a datacenter. The video hit a nerve: insane enough at the first sight, yet kind of rational if you know what we know now.
Unboxing Macs at scale for our new server racks.
So today I want to give some background into what it takes to build custom Mac racks, how we can start macOS instances from scratch in seconds and deliver new Xcode versions mere hours after Apple releases them.
So why MacBooks?
Because our customers need Macs. And because Apple didn’t give us another option.
Many of our customers build and test iOS apps. You can't build iOS apps without a Mac. The iOS Simulator only runs on a Mac. Moreover, in order to release an app to the App Store, Apple requires using a recent Xcode version.xtoolxtool is cool, but it is not (yet) a serious replacement. So your coding agent needs a Mac.
But still, why laptops? Isn’t it a major waste of screen pixels and keyboard buttons and battery ions? Well yes, Mac Mini would be a better choice for a datacenter. Sure, it has very rudimentary remote management, no redundant power, and a beautiful case that ensures that cooling will be difficult regardless of which side you lay it on. But these are all known challenges that we have learned to manage.
But have you actually tried to order a couple hundred Minis? We have. Ordered in January, delivered in July. Welcome to the world of 2026 when the supply chains are in disarray. Never mind that Apple doesn’t release updated CPU models to all devices at once. So Mac Mini didn’t get M5 cores for 10 months (and then suddenly got M6 before any other device model!). We promise the best and the newest to our customers so we had to be inventive. That’s how the MacBook-in-Datacenter project was born.
Our beautiful Mac racks
Good design takes iterations; and we surely didn’t get everything right from the first try. But I think we have the system nailed down.
Every MacBook is connected to an IP KVM for remote management. Indispensable when dealing with laptops. Unlike Mac Mini, laptop firmware is designed with the screen in mind: some maintenance actions can only be done by clicking buttons in the beautiful GUI.
Of course, every MacBook gets an external 10G Ethernet NIC. Many folks at Namespace are networking geeks and we are proud of the connection speed and reliability that we provide to customers.
And then there is power. So in total, four cables per laptop, forty-eight per shelf, plus twelve for Ethernet, plus KVM wiring. Let’s just say that careful cable management is essential.
Heat management too. Currently we are deploying custom-made holders, designed to wick the heat from the hotspots and guide hot air away instead of blowing it at the nearby machines.
Not the problems we expected: HDMI, FileVault, and USB NICs
Naturally, we expected problems and challenges. Just not where they appeared.
I bet some of you looked at the pic above, saw MagSafe cables plugged in and already started writing a snarky tweet that MagSafe is not safe and may get accidentally disconnected.
And yes, I was worried about that too. But the reality is that we have seen very few cases of MagSafe disconnections.
The most unreliable cable? HDMI! Often thick and inflexible. Tends to fall out every time you touch the shelf.
Luckily by now we found almost perfect cables that bend exactly as we want them to bend. And we bought the entire supply of them. There are zero more of them available to order on Amazon.
Another source of pain: FileVault disk encryption. Or rather decryption. When a MacBook reboots (in an unplanned fashion) it prompts for a password to unlock the local disk. The prompt is shown on the screen (of a closed laptop somewhere in the rack, doh). No problem, we thought: we have the KVM connected just for this case!
Nope, not so easy. The password prompt disappears from the external screen after 5 minutes of inactivity. Then we remembered that macOS Tahoe introduced a useful feature: we could unlock FileVault remotely using SSH protocol. Still no luck. On laptops it expires after 5 minutes too. Looks like the only way out of this state is to reboot by physically pressing the button and racing to unlock in time.Mac rebootWhile on this topic, a small tip: you can reboot a Mac in a way that will keep the disk unlocked when you need it: fdesetup authrestart.
And then there are simply bugs. Under certain conditions, an external USB NIC stops working and acts as if it is not powered and shows no link. Trying another cable, another NIC, another switch port, no luck. But a quick visit to Network Preferences, deleting and recreating the “network service” in MacOS Settings brings it back to life.
What about Mac Minis and Studios?
At the moment we actually have it easy: M5 and M6 Mac Minis and Studios are coming into our fleet soon. They are way simpler to manage in the DC: they have a built-in 10 Gb network card, they boot up automatically after a power cycle and the OS can be configured entirely automatically via MDM.
But Namespace has some special sauce for the Minis too. We design custom-made shelves that hold the machines with focus on efficient cooling. We have tested a few designs using airflow simulation to arrive at what we are deploying now.
In the end installing Mac Minis is a breeze: unpack them, throw 10 pieces into the holder, connect power and network and press the power button once (famously inconveniently located). From there on automation takes care of them.
Virtualizing Macs
Under the hood a Namespace instance is backed by a virtual machine. We have multiple virtual machine engines integrated into a unified platform to run Linux, Windows, and Mac instances in the most efficient way. This way we can provide the same features that make Namespace special, like cache volumes, telemetry, or VPC connections.
Unsurprisingly, our Mac solution is based on Apple’s excellent Virtualization framework. It is an embeddable and flexible virtual machine engine. It’s easiest to compare it to Firecracker in how it fits the system architecture: it implements generic VM operations end-to-end as well as typical peripherals.
For completeness, Apple also provides a lower-level Hypervisor framework, which is comparable to the KVM API of Linux. For instance QEMU uses it on macOS under the hood. Hypervisor provides a way to execute machine code in isolation, but requires the application developer to implement the bulk of machine architecture and peripherals. It could give us a lot of control, but unfortunately it cannot run macOS (it requires an Apple proprietary environment that third parties cannot, or shouldn’t, try to recreate).
In fact, most competing platforms are built on the same foundation. But the details matter: Apple gives us a few primitives that need to be arranged in just the right way to work fast and be secure. The more interesting thing is to watch how different people solve similar problems with different constraints.
Limitations of Apple Virtualization
A well-known limitation is that Apple only allows two macOS VMs per physical Mac. It can be a Mac Pro with 24 cores and 192 GB memory, yet it is limited to running only two guest VMs. This limitation leaks into our product offering: we can only slice Mac resources in two halves. So we run instances with 6 or 12 cores on 14-core Mac Minis and 8/16-core instances on 18-core MacBooks (we reserve a couple cores for management overhead).
An important consideration of Virtualization VMs is that the virtual CPU is executed by a separate OS process (VMM process in the diagram) from the software integrating Virtualization (here Namespace VM host). If we want to hook some VM behavior or implement custom virtual devices, every interaction with them requires an IPC roundtrip between the VM process and the “host” process. Such context switches are unavoidable and need to be taken into account when designing the system.
Virtual networking
Virtualization framework offers a few ways to connect a virtual machine to the network. For instance, bridged and NAT networking modes route traffic directly from the VMM process to the host network interfaces. These are suitable for VMs running on a local computer where the workload is trusted.
Namespace instances run untrusted code and we need to enforce policies on what a VM can or cannot access (these policies can also be customer-defined!). Also we provide a few additional services to the instances that should appear “as if” they were on the local network for the guest system.
This requires us to take full control of guest networking in the mode where we process every packet that comes out and into the VM in software. We based our guest networking on a userspace TCP/IP stack from Google gVisor project and use it to implement an IP gateway/firewall for the instances. This way we minimize exposure of the host OS to unprocessed packets controlled by the guest.
Network packet handling needs to be very efficient, but as outlined above the path involves IPC. The VMM process needs first to pass the packets to the “VM host” process, which then processes and passes them to the network interface. It takes careful implementation and batch processing wherever possible to minimize the number of IPC roundtrips.
The above approach allows Namespace MacOS instances to reach 4 Gbps upstream bandwidth (per Fast.com). This is unfortunately still lower than the line rate. We have been exploring alternative approaches, including ideas on how to avoid IPC for network processing entirely. But productionizing the new setup is still left for the future. After all, 4 Gbps is still quite respectable.
VM images
Creating your first VM using Apple Virtualization is very easy: download a macOS installer XIP, use UTM/Tart/any of the dozens of open-source Virtualization wrappers to start a machine, click through Setup Assistant, install Xcode and you are good to go. Now you have a VM image that you can fork and run any workload locally.
But you need to test on multiple versions of iOS, so you install a few iOS runtimes. And then you install the upcoming Xcode beta version (and new runtimes too). And before you know it your VM image has grown to 500 GB (iOS runtime packages are huge).
You also want to have the previous version of macOS for testing that one little thing. Another 500 GB right here. Apple releases the new macOS developer preview, one more image.
And then you realize that the Xcode beta version subtly breaks the non-beta Xcodes on the same system (true story!). After all, Xcode installation bumps the “global” versions of CoreDevice and CoreSimulator. Hence any bugs in the beta Xcode simulator are visible when you’re using ostensibly stable Xcode versions. So now you are maintaining image versions with and without the pre-release Xcodes.
And now you have 2 TB of VM images. On what? A 2 TB MacBook hard drive?
That’s the challenge we faced: we need to build, distribute, and store huge images across the fleet of hundreds of machines.
Build process
Building images is a repeatable process so that we can reliably produce new images when Apple releases new software versions. Building is driven by a script that replicates installation and configuration as a human user would do it (e.g. the build script can run shell commands, click UI buttons or reboot the VM). Wherever possible we stick to using controls designed by Apple to configure the VMs in order to avoid surprising behaviours inconsistent with what a typical local user would be seeing. Naturally, building images is an automated and repeatable process. It is driven by a workflow expressed as a sequence of operations in a YAML file. Operations can be VM control (e.g. reboot), running a shell script or programmatic interaction with the system or setup UI over VNC.
Resulting VM images are handed over to Namespace internal Image Registry, in fact the same one that handles Linux and Windows image storage, replication and distribution (covered in the excellent article by Matteo). Disk images are of course quite different from normal container images: OCI layers are simple tarballs of files, while disks are generally flat arrays of bytes. Very large arrays in fact. And to a large extent they contain empty space: that’s the disk space that would be available to users as free space.
Naturally, it would be very wasteful to transfer and store the “empty” data in the registry. So we developed a simple format that allows us to preserve the “sparse-ness” of the images when stored in the registry. Unallocated spans of the image take just a few bytes.
And there is another important optimization. Remember the example scenario mentioned in the VM Images section: we have an image of the same system that differs only in addition of an extra Xcode installation. Obviously the latter image is built using the former as a base and most of the bytes are unchanged.
Our storage format preserves the “shallow copy” relationship and stores such images as multiple layers: the base layer is shared between them, while subsequent layers only contain the modified blocks.
Distribution
At this point we have the images in an OCI registry now. But of course Virtualization framework cannot start a VM directly using a disk residing in the registry. It needs to have something on the node itself: a VM disk can be backed by either an image file on the local host SSD, or it can route disk I/O requests to a server using Network Block Device (NBD) protocol. The latter would allow us to intelligently serve highly demanded data from a local cache, while conserving on-device space by not storing unneeded blocks.
But NBD has the same drawback as userspace networking from above: every I/O operation would incur an IPC roundtrip at minimum, including buffer copying and context switches. You see the same pattern as with networking: a very direct hardwired and fast option and an indirect “software-defined” but disappointingly slow option.
At Namespace we value performance a lot, so the choice is clear: we’ll serve the images from the local disk. We need to materialize them from OCI images in the registry on the SSD of every node in the fleet. 500 gig images to hundreds and thousands of nodes. And we need to do it fast.
Obviously, every node naively downloading from the central registry was not going to work. With the example numbers we are talking about half a petabyte of traffic transferred within, conservatively, tens of minutes. The registry (and the network fabric) would need to serve terabits per second!
The bytes that we are distributing are the same going to every node so the obvious solution is to organize a peer-to-peer delivery of these blobs. Each block only needs to be downloaded from the registry once by some node. Then another node that is close by (by certain metric) can download the block directly from the peer and we have two copies. So two more nodes can pull these bytes and so on. The fleet is exponentially flooded.BitTorrentObviously, BitTorrent was a heavy inspiration for this design. But unlike BitTorrent, which works in a public network of untrusted peers, we could make different tradeoffs leading to better efficiency and predictability. But that’s a topic for another post.
Storage
Now the bytes are on the node disk. But remember the storage optimizations we did in the Build Process? With the naive approach of storing the images on disk there are a lot of bytes that are useless: they are either holes or could be shared with another image.
Some of you probably know that these are exactly the types of storage optimization techniques that are possible with modern file systems, namely APFS.ZFSLinux users have seen the same features in ZFS.
Using these cool features is also pretty easy: open a new file for writing, seek to offset 100G, write a block. And there you just made a file with a large hole in it. Only the block you wrote is allocated on disk, the rest is 100 GB of imaginary zeroes. When reading the file you won’t even notice the holes. The OS will return actual zeros.
% truncate -s 1g hole.bin
% dd if=/dev/random of=hole.bin bs=4k seek=256k count=256 
% ls -lh hole.bin
-rw-r--r--  1 kirill  staff   1.0G Sep 29 05:36 hole.bin
% du -h hole.bin
 1M	hole.bin
Sharing the blocks is similarly transparent: just use the cp -c mode or clonefile syscall. The new file will share the same disk blocks and essentially not take any space.
Writing to the cloned file is also transparent: as soon as you try to overwrite some blocks, these particular blocks will be allocated on the disk, while the shared portion will remain shared.
What’s next?
The pace at which we are expanding our fleet is increasing and the experience from all the above has transformed into a repeatable process. We know exactly how long it takes to bring a MacBook rack into prod. The rack assembly line is dialed in. DCOps people are trained. Disk images are built and distributed. We can bring whatever number of machines our customers need into the fleet when we need to (well, as long as we can purchase them at all).
We can still do better! What if there was a “holy-grail” device to host a shelf of MacBooks, providing power, ethernet and KVM connections over a single USB-C cable? It should be possible, yet there is currently no hardware on the open market that satisfies our requirements. So we are working on something very custom.
Or maybe we’ll do another crazy thing? What if we deploy phones to the datacenter? See what the future brings on our X soon!

articles.title: GUI64 – GUI for the Commodore 64 running on top of the built-in ROM
articles.body:
GUI64
Description[edit | edit source]
GUI64 is a graphical user interface (GUI) for the C64, first released in version 1.0 in November 2024. Although GUI64 may appear to be a standalone operating system, it is just a graphical layer running on top of the C64’s built-in ROM-based operating system, the Kernal. GUI64 presents files and directories in freely movable windows, allowing for easy file management on floppy disks as well as on disk images stored on SD2IEC devices. When GUI64 is running on an Ultimate device, all settings are saved, and disk images can be mounted directly from within the GUI. The current version of GUI64 is 2.0.The current version of GUI64 is 2.1.
Operation[edit | edit source]
GUI64 can be operated using a mouse (such as the 1351 or compatible models) connected to Control Port #1, or with a joystick in Control Port #2 (right click with CBM key + fire). To enable support for the mouse wheel—e.g., for scrolling or in up/down controls (see below)—the Micromys adapter must be used. This functionality is also available when using the VICE emulator.
Look and Feel[edit | edit source]
Starting with version 1.9, GUI64 is available in two variants:
Windows-like interface
In this variant, GUI64 visually resembles Windows-style interfaces. The GUI is window-based, with a taskbar at the bottom of the screen, featuring a "Commodore (CBM) button" embedded on the left and a recessed clock button on the right. In between are the task buttons — similar to those in Windows 95.
Mac-like interface
This variant visually imitates the interface of the first Macintosh computers from Apple. The menus are not integrated into the windows but are displayed in a menu bar at the top edge of the screen. The system menu in the upper-left corner includes, in addition to the entries from the corresponding CBM menu in the Windows variant, an “About” entry, which in the Windows variant is part of the file browser’s menu.
In both versions, the desktop itself is empty except for two drive icons in the upper-left corner (in the Mac design: upper-right corner), and—unlike other interfaces such as C64OS[1] or GEOS—does not support placing file icons directly on it. Instead, the desktop serves as a background for windows, which can be freely moved and positioned. Unlike GEOS, for example, GUI64 does not use the VIC-II’s bitmap graphics mode, but operates in text mode. GUI64 is therefore character set–based. For instance, windows cannot be moved pixel-perfectly, but are instead aligned to the 8×8-pixel grid of the character screen. The desktop consists of 22 rows (in the Mac design: 24 rows) and 40 columns of characters. Strictly speaking, GUI64 should therefore be considered not a GUI, but a TUI (Text User Interface).
Elements on the Desktop and in the Taskbar[edit | edit source]
Drive Icons[edit | edit source]
By default, the two drive icons are assigned to device numbers 8 and 9, but this can be changed via right-click on the icons or, alternatively, in the menu of the associated browser window. A double-click on a drive icon opens a file browser window, see below.
Ultimate Icon[edit | edit source]
If an Ultimate cartridge is connected to the C64, or if the computer itself is an Ultimate device, and if the Ultimate Command Interface is enabled, a third desktop icon in the shape of a USB flash drive has been available since version 1.98: the Ultimate icon. Double-clicking this icon opens a browser window that provides access to the file system of a USB flash drive (or SD card) connected to the Ultimate device, allowing disk images to be mounted directly from within GUI64.
[edit | edit source]
Clicking the Commodore button in the lower-left corner of the taskbar opens a menu with three entries: "Settings", "About", and "BASIC". Starting with version 1.98, Ultimate owners will also see an additional "Reboot" entry, which reboots the C64. Selecting "BASIC" (after confirming the prompt) launches the familiar C64 BASIC editor. Clicking "Settings" opens a configuration window where the appearance of GUI64 can be customized. If GUI64 detects an Ultimate system with the Command Interface enabled, the settings are stored in the Ultimate's flash folder as of version 1.97. These settings include various color options as well as an option to display the desktop with a dotted background. Clicking "About" opens a dialog containing information about GUI64.
Time[edit | edit source]
Since version 1.96, the clock automatically displays the Ultimate's time (provided an Ultimate cartridge is connected or the C64 is FPGA-based on an Ultimate 64 board and the Ultimate Command Interface is enabled). Since version 2.0, the clock also displays the correct time when a WiC64 module is connected to the user port. Double-clicking the clock opens a dialog box for adjusting the time. If no Ultimate system or WiC64 is detected when GUI64 starts, the time is set to “00:00” by default.
Tooltips[edit | edit source]
Because the GUI64 screen has limited horizontal space, taskbar button titles are truncated to fit. Starting with GUI64 v1.8.1, users can see the full title in a tooltip by hovering over a button for at least one second. Tooltips are also displayed when hovering over desktop drive icons, showing the full path for drives such as SD2IEC or the Ultimate.
Graphical Elements on the Desktop[edit | edit source]
Windows[edit | edit source]
The primary graphical elements that convey information in GUI64 are windows. Each window has a title bar at the top, with the window title on the left (Mac design: centered). In the Windows design, there are various control buttons on the right. One of these buttons is always an X-icon (X) to close the window; if the window supports minimizing or maximizing, corresponding buttons for those actions are also present. In the Mac version, there is only a button for closing the window on the left-hand side of the title bar. Windows-version: A minimized window disappears from the desktop but remains accessible as a button in the taskbar. Clicking this button restores the window to the desktop. This helps keep the desktop organized and clutter-free.
A special type of window is the dialog. Dialogs cannot be minimized and always retain full focus. This means that user input is restricted to within the dialog window only.
Controls[edit | edit source]
The graphical elements within windows are called controls. Each of these controls serves a specific function—even if that function is simply displaying text, as is the case with labels (see below). The controls available in the current version of GUI64 are, in order:
Functionality[edit | edit source]
GUI64 allows users to work with drives and files. The following drives are detected and supported: Commodore 1541 floppy drive, Commodore 1571 floppy drive, Commodore 1581 floppy drive, and SD2IEC devices. GUI64 may also work with hard drives and other storage devices; however, due to a lack of testing, reliable functionality for these cannot be guaranteed at this time.
Double-clicking one of the drive icons on the desktop opens a file browser window, which—after loading—displays the contents of the medium (floppy disk, SD2IEC directory, or disk image within an SD2IEC directory). GUI64 can also handle dnp images. Files and directories are listed vertically within the window. Each entry shows the file type (as an icon), the file name, and, optionally, the file size (see the "View Menu" below). Entries can be selected by clicking on them. The list can be scrolled by either using the scrollbar on the right edge or the mouse wheel.
Running Programs[edit | edit source]
To run programs (equivalent to LOAD"...",x and RUN), a simple double-click on the corresponding entry in the drive window is required. This will display a progress bar in a seperate window, showing the loading progress. Once the file is loaded into the C64's memory, the file will be executed. To load a machine code file (without a BASIC stub, such as 10 SYS 2063), see "Boot" in the File menu. Note: GUI64 will not remain in the background after running a file and has to be loaded back into memory afterwards, e.g. by pressing the Reset button if GUI64 was loaded from cartridge.
Opening Directories and Disk Images on SD2IEC Drives[edit | edit source]
When the file browser window displays the contents of a directory on an SD2IEC drive, directories and disk images (if available) will also be shown. Directories are represented by a folder-like icon. A double-click on a directory or disk image initiates a loading process, after which the contents of the selected directory or disk image will be displayed in the browser window.
Menus[edit | edit source]
Each file browser window in GUI64 has a menu consisting of the entries "Disk," "File," and "View." These menus provide the user with various options for manipulating drives, files, and directories.
The Disk Menu[edit | edit source]
The 'Disk' menu in GUI64 allows users to manipulate floppy disks (or disk images) and view information about the drive at the corresponding device number.
The File Menu[edit | edit source]
The 'File' menu of GUI64 allows for copying or 'cutting' files, as well as deleting, renaming, viewing, booting files, and creating disk images.
*Note: After creating a new image, the corresponding virtual disk needs to be formatted. For this, double click the image, click Format in the Disk menu and choose Full Format.
The View Menu[edit | edit source]
With the entries in the 'View' menu, the display in the file browser window can be changed.
Applications[edit | edit source]
Currently, there are no applications for GUI64. However, after the release of version 2.0, an interface for developers is planned, which will allow for the easy creation of applications for GUI64.
Development[edit | edit source]
GUI64 was developed by Friedrich (Fritz) Philipp, also known as WebFritzi. Especially during the implementation of the drive functions, he received valuable support from numerous members of Forum64, who assisted him with advice and guidance. Some code snippets originate from Codebase64.

articles.title: Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology
articles.body:
Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability gates agentic analytics: a revenue metric answered faster is worth nothing if the number is wrong. Agents need a context layer that tells them where data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is an open library that builds that layer from enterprise metadata, reconciles definitions across systems, and exposes it to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. It complements the semantic models customers already own.
It enables developers to:
- Discover: generate enterprise ontologies from metadata; connect existing ontologies and semantic models; build AI-ready knowledge graphs.
- Ground: give agents trusted business meaning for metrics, entities, and relationships; reconcile inconsistent definitions across systems.
- Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage; return provenance with every answer.
- Expose: serve context to any agent harness through MCP, CLI, and API. Learn: fold certified corrections and usage back into the ontology, so shared context improves with every question.
To run a text-to-SQL benchmark such as BIRD, refer to the ontology SQL evaluation repository.
Licensing & contributions. Auto Ontology is distributed under the
Apache License 2.0. Third-party open-source components
bundled, linked, or otherwise used by this project are listed in
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. This project
is currently not accepting external contributions.
- Natural-language querying of structured data — questions are translated to SQL and executed against connected databases, powered by NVIDIA NIM.
- Semantic catalog / ontology layer over relational sources, stored in Postgres alongside the catalog it describes.
- Authentication & RBAC —using Better Auth.
- Web UI for chat, analysis, data catalog, analytics, and settings.
- Flexible deployment — Helm chart for Kubernetes or Docker Compose for a local stack.
Auto Ontology uses NVIDIA NIM endpoints for inference — either the hosted
NVIDIA API catalog (integrate.api.nvidia.com) or
self-hosted NIMs. The defaults in .env.example are:
- LLM: nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b
- Embeddings: nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b
- Reranking: nvidia/llama-nemotron-rerank-vl-1b-v2
The endpoints and models are configured via the DEFAULT_MODELS_ENDPOINT, DEFAULT_MODELS_MODEL,
EMBED_ENDPOINT, and EMBED_MODEL environment variables and require a
DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY.
Each model role is configured by a triplet of environment variables —
<PREFIX>_ENDPOINT (URL), <PREFIX>_API_KEY, and <PREFIX>_MODEL:
You can set a full triplet, only some of its fields, or none at all — any field
left unset falls back to the matching DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD>. So the simplest
setup is to fill in DEFAULT_MODELS_* and override per-triplet fields only where
they differ (e.g. EMBED_MODEL, NON_REASONING_MODEL). *_API_KEY also falls
back to the legacy NVIDIA_API_KEY for backward compatibility.
- Docker with Docker Compose v2 (e.g. Docker Desktop on macOS/Windows,
Docker Engine on Linux) for the local stack. For Kubernetes deployments see
DEPLOYMENT.md.
- An NVIDIA API key (nvapi-...) for NVIDIA NIM (chat and ingestion) from
the NVIDIA API catalog at https://build.nvidia.com.
- Connection details for the source database(s) you want to query (Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake, or DuckDB).
Kubernetes
To deploy Auto Ontology on a Kubernetes cluster, see DEPLOYMENT.md.
Local (Docker Compose)
- Clone the repository: git clone <repo-url> auto_ontology && cd auto_ontology
- Create your environment file (.env) from the template and fill in the values
(Postgres credentials, DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY, CONNECTION_STRINGS, etc.).
See .env.example for the full list of variables:
cp .env.example .env
# edit .env Note: 
  - AUTH_SECRET and APP_URL are required — without them every page
fails with a Better Auth "default secret" error.
  - POSTGRES_PORT only changes the host-side port mapping (set it if
5432 is already taken on your machine); containers always reach Postgres
on the internal network port.
- Build the images and start the stack: docker compose up -d --build This builds the backend (auto_ontology) and frontend (auto-ontology-frontend) images, brings
up Postgres and pgAdmin, runs the one-shot frontend-migrate job to
sync the database schema, and starts the app (backend, ingestion service,
and frontend).
- Open the UI at http://localhost:3000 (the backend API is on :3001,
pgAdmin on :5050).
Troubleshooting: if the UI loads without the left navigation panel
(or otherwise looks broken after a restart), your browser is holding a
stale session cookie — this happens when AUTH_SECRET changes or the
database is reset. Clear the site data for localhost:3000 (or delete
the better-auth.session_token cookie) and sign in again.
Auto Ontology resolves the source databases it connects to from two sources:
- Added through the UI — connections created from within the app. With this option the connection credentials are stored in plaintext in Postgres unless Vault is configured: 
  - Without Vault: the full connection object (including the password) is JSON-serialized and stored, unencrypted, on the catalog's database row.
  - With Vault: the credentials are written to Vault, keyed by the database name, and the catalog row stores no credentials (the database name is the lookup key — there is no separate reference field).
Vault is enabled only when all of VAULT_ADDR, VAULT_NAMESPACE, VAULT_ROLE_ID, and VAULT_SECRET_ID are set (VAULT_AUTH_MOUNT and VAULT_KV_MOUNT are optional overrides). It is off by default; a partial
configuration is ignored with a warning and falls back to plaintext storage.
- CONNECTION_STRINGS environment variable — a comma-separated list of
connection strings supplied at deploy time (e.g. the Helm --set connectionStrings=<CONNECTION-STRINGS> flag). This is a fallback: it
is used only when there are no UI-added connections.
Auto Ontology Supports SSO for authentication. The Redirect URI should be configured in the IdP as: APP_URL/api/auth/sso/callback
A browser signs in and gets a session cookie, which a script cannot obtain. For scripts, notebooks, and scheduled jobs, mint an API token instead:
- Open the user menu (top right) → API Tokens → New token.
- Name it, optionally pick an expiry (default: never), and copy the token. Auto Ontology stores only a SHA-256 hash of it, so it is shown exactly once. Losing it means minting a new one.
Send it as x-api-key on any /api/... call — Authorization: Bearer <token>
works too:
curl -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/termsimport os
import requests
session = requests.Session()
session.headers["x-api-key"] = os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]
terms = session.get("https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/terms").json()
answer = session.post(
    "https://auto_ontology.example.com/api/chat/completions",
    json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"},
).json()
Things worth knowing:
- A token acts as its owner. It carries no permissions of its own — every call is authorized against the owner's role, exactly as it would be in the browser. A viewer's token cannot do admin things.
- The whole API surface accepts it. Authentication is resolved in one place
(frontend/auth/resolve-user.ts) for every route, so any endpoint in docs/openapi/auto-ontology-api.json that is not withPublic works with a token.
- Revocation is immediate. Delete the token in the UI, or delete/ban the owning user, and the next request with it gets a 401.
- Tokens cannot manage tokens. Creating and revoking requires a signed-in session, so a leaked token cannot issue itself successors.
Public clients call the authenticated Next.js gateway at
POST /api/chat/completions. The response is an SSE stream containing step,
result, or error events, followed by [DONE].
conversation_id is optional:
- Omit it for a stateless, one-shot request.
- Supply a client-generated UUID to create or continue a conversation.
- Reuse the same UUID for every turn in the thread. Wait for [DONE] before
sending the next turn; overlapping requests for one conversation return 409 Conversation in progress.
{
  "question": "What about last month?",
  "conversation_id": "d61d8aa3-d496-4fa7-97ce-4f831c162e7f"
}
For conversational requests, FastAPI loads up to the five most recent completed turns (bounded to 12,000 characters) and rewrites contextual input such as “What about August?” into a standalone question before running the existing text-to-SQL graph. Independent questions are passed through unchanged. Internal agent thoughts, chart payloads, errors, and raw SQL result sets are not reused as context.
Conversation history is scoped to the authenticated Auto Ontology user. Browser and
service callers should use the Next.js gateway, which resolves the user and
forwards the internal x-auto-ontology-user-id header to FastAPI. The FastAPI port is a
trusted internal service boundary: it must not be exposed publicly because that
header is not independently verified by FastAPI. A direct FastAPI request
without conversation_id remains stateless; a direct request with
conversation_id requires the trusted identity header.
The web UI manages the UUID automatically. An API-created conversation can be
opened in the UI at /chat?focus=<conversation_id> when it belongs to the
signed-in user.
Coding agents: start at AGENTS.md. Skills live in
skills/ (nvidia-ontology-setup, nvidia-ontology-management, nvidia-ontology-query).
Maintainers keep using CLAUDE.md.
Agent harnesses such as Cursor and Claude Desktop can query your data through
Auto Ontology's MCP server. See
mcp/ to run it and docs/mcp.md for the details.
Auto Ontology is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0.
SPDX identifier: Apache-2.0.
Each NVIDIA-authored source file in this repository carries an SPDX header of the form:
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2024-2026, NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES.
All rights reserved.
SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
Third-party open-source components used by Auto Ontology are enumerated, with their
upstream licenses and project URLs, in
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md. Components added by the
container images are listed separately in
CONTAINER_THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.
NOTICE AND DISCLAIMER: This software automatically retrieves, accesses or interacts with external materials. Those retrieved materials are not distributed with this software and are governed solely by separate terms, conditions and licenses. You are solely responsible for finding, reviewing and complying with all applicable terms, conditions, and licenses, and for verifying the security, integrity and suitability of any retrieved materials for your specific use case. The author makes no representations or warranties regarding any retrieved materials, and assumes no liability for any losses, damages, liabilities or legal consequences from your use or inability to use this software or any retrieved materials. Use this software and the retrieved materials at your own risk.
External materials Auto Ontology interacts with at run time:
This project is currently not accepting contributions. Issues, pull
requests, and patches submitted from outside the Auto Ontology maintainer team will
not be reviewed or merged. Security-relevant reports should follow the
process described in SECURITY.md. Maintainer workflow is in
CONTRIBUTING.md.

articles.title: Study estimates 75% of NFL players who died over 15-year span had CTE
articles.body:
An estimated 75% of professional football players who died over a 15-year span had signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, a study published Wednesday found.
It’s the highest estimate to date. Most recently, a study published in August by the same group estimated that one-quarter of NFL players who died in a five-year span had CTE. The new study, published in JAMA Network Open, put the figure at three times higher.
Not all people with signs of CTE in the brain go on to experience cognitive decline or dementia, and some people may never experience symptoms at all. A smaller proportion of the former players in the analysis were estimated to have dementia, about 27%, the study found.
The results were surprising, said study leader Yorghos Tripodis, the director of statistics and data management at the Boston University Alzheimer’s Disease and CTE Center. In an emailed statement, an NFL spokesperson said, in part, that the league “continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts.”

When a person’s head jolts during an impact, the brain — which is suspended in fluid inside the skull — can slam into the skull or twist, said Dr. Julian Bailes, chair of the neurosurgery department at Endeavor Health in the Chicago area. In total, the researchers looked at data from 396 donated brains, plus information from 1,966 other deceased former NFL players. They factored in the ages of death along with estimated rates of mild cognitive impairment and dementia in former NFL players older than 50.
About 93% of the donated brains had signs of CTE, which shows up as structural damage in the brain. The research team calculated that the families of players with symptoms of cognitive decline were about five times likelier to donate brains than the families of players without symptoms and then performed a statistical analysis to correct for that bias.

From there, they estimated that among the roughly 2,360 former players who died during the 15-year time frame, about 1,760, or nearly 75%, had CTE. In comparison, only about 1% of brains donated to banks in the U.S., Austria and Brazil have signs of the disease, the researchers said.
But plenty of people with signs of CTE never develop symptoms, Tripodis said.
The researchers estimated that 27% of the 2,360 players studied had dementia.
The dementia “can be from all causes,” Tripodis said. “But it is very likely that in this specific population that CTE is causing dementia.”
Reducing impacts
Until doctors figure out a way to diagnose CTE while people are still alive, any studies quantifying how many people have the condition will be estimates, said Dr. Jim Kelly, a professor emeritus of neurology at the University of Colorado Anschutz.
“These are all estimates. They had no autopsies on five times as many players who died as they did have autopsies for,” said Kelly, who wasn’t involved in the research.
Some of the autopsies may also have revealed just one or a couple of lesions associated with CTE, “and it seems unlikely that that would lead to anything in terms of a behavior change or dementia,” he said.
Those are difficult studies to do, Bailes agreed. They seek to determine “how many people out there have a condition when not all of them are symptomatic,” he said, adding that the findings are a call for more research into diagnosing CTE in people who are still living.
“If you can’t tell if someone has a certain disease until they’re dead, you really can’t help them,” he said.
In the meantime, prevention is key, Tripodis said: “If you reduce the number of brain injuries, brain impacts, you substantially decrease the risk.”
The NFL has already implemented measures to try to reduce the number of high-impact hits players face. They include redesigned helmets — such as the Guardian Cap — and the dynamic kickoff rule, which leads to lower collision speeds.

articles.title: How to write comparison content that doesn't age like milk
articles.body:
How to write comparison content that doesn't age like milk
Contents
Every marketing lead I talk with sees potential of comparison content, but also see it as a double-edged sword they're not comfortable investing in.
The hesitation usually comes from some mix of (1) it feels unnatural to give your competitors their flowers on your own website, and (2) comparison pages come with maintenance overhead nobody wants to deal with.
Competitors ship things, change their pricing, get acquired (or acquire others), and all of a sudden the article you wrote in March is outdated in June.
So how do you walk the line between being fair (complimentary, even) to your competitors while still capturing demand & showing off your product's strengths? And how do you keep the content accurate once it's out in the world to avoid spreading misinformation?
Both are worth figuring out if you want to write comparison content that doesn't get dunked on. And both are things I'm here to give some answers to based on our experience writing comparison content at PostHog.
Why bother with comparison content?
Because it works.
Since 2021, over 25k people have signed up for PostHog after reading a comparison. Almost 50% did it within 24 hours of reading; ~75% within 30 days.
It makes sense why they overperform. Someone searching for this style of content has already decided they need something, the only question left is which one. Comparison content sits at the sweet spot in the funnel where that decision gets made, and your job is to help make it (ideally in your favour, but not always and that's okay. More on that later).
Our credentials
Technically, our first comparison was a roundup. The best open source analytics tools went live in October 2021 and is still our single most-read piece of comparison content, at 150k+ pageviews and counting.
It set the template for the early days: "best open source X" for session replay, A/B testing, and feature flags. Open source was one of our wedges, so that's what we compared on.
The first head-to-head, PostHog vs Amplitude, followed in May 2022. It still gets a few hundred readers a month, which is more than I can say for most things we published back in 2022. Matomo and Mixpanel came next.
2023 was the year it became a thing. Every new PostHog product came with a new set of competitors. Session Replay brought Hotjar, FullStory, and LogRocket. Feature Flags brought LaunchDarkly, GrowthBook, and Statsig. Web Analytics brought GA4.
We went from three to fourteen in a year, and the maintenance problem flared up. Three pages you can keep accurate by hand; fourteen, each with a feature table and pricing that changes every quarter, not so much. It's, to this day, a workflow we're constantly working on solving for and improving.
2024 was the alternatives year. A lot of our competitors got a "best X alternatives" piece: Hotjar, Statsig, Plausible, Matomo, and about fifteen more. We also launched error tracking, wrote PostHog vs Sentry in August, and watched it become our most-read head-to-head of all time within two years.
2025 and 2026 followed the products; Best Sentry alternatives and best error tracking tools for error tracking, best open source LLM observability tools for AI observability, and best Datadog alternatives as the first hint of what was coming next. Most recently we started doubling down on our observability stack: PostHog vs Langfuse and a full set of AI observability roundups (best AI observability tools, plus Langfuse, LangSmith, and Braintrust alternatives). Then logs: best log monitoring tools, Grafana Loki and Splunk alternatives, and PostHog vs Datadog.
This isn't an AEO fad for us; we were writing comparison content BeFoRe iT wAs cOoL, back when the answer engine was a guy named Greg on Stack Overflow.
And while they have shapeshifted plenty since then, we've stayed true to two principles:
- Do no harm. We don't trash-talk competitors, we don't straw-man them, and we admit when and where they're better than us. No sneaky shit, as our handbook puts it.
- Respect the reader's intelligence, and meet them where they are. A developer comparing tools is smart, busy, and already halfway towards a decision. Give them the answer as accurately and as directly as possible, and let them make the right call for their product and use case. Also, they can tell if you're generating AI slop comparisons, it's a bad look.
Be the comparison page you'd want to read
PostHog doesn't have every feature every competitor has (yet), and we're fine admitting it. Our credibility with the reader is worth more than whatever we'd "win" by fudging the truth.
We're not the solution for everyone. We are the best solution for someone (a lot of someones, actually), and the job is capturing their attention. Which means you will, occasionally, lose a deal on your own website: someone reads PostHog vs Competitor, concludes Competitor is the better fit, and goes and buys Competitor. We wish them godspeed and focus on our ICP anyway.
In practice, this means picking up a few uncomfortable habits:
Acknowledge your gaps and credit their wins.
"If you need X, they do it better than we do today" is a sentence you'll find on our pages. Softening it with what's coming is fine (a roadmap link, a "we're working on it"), as long as you're clear about where you are right now for the readers deciding today.
For example, earlier this year our articles admitted we were weaker on APM because we hadn't shipped distributed tracing or metrics yet. True at the time. We've since shipped a full APM suite, and the articles now say that instead. Our content matches our shipping, not just our ambitions.
Readers don't think less of you for crediting a competitor; they think more. It's the cheapest trust signal in content marketing, and almost nobody uses it. And as AI eats everything else about content, trust is one of the few things left you can't generate. Say the nice thing.
There's another reader to keep in mind, too: LLMs. When someone asks Claude "PostHog vs Sentry for a Next.js app," we assume the model pulls from sources it judges to be balanced. So be balanced. You want to read as a source, not an ad.
Being honest used to be a brand decision (one we've proudly stood behind), but now it might be a distribution decision too.
Write a "who should pick them" section.
If you can't write a fair paragraph about where your competitor wins and who they might work better for, you don't understand them well enough to compare. Go read their docs.
It's also the place to be honest about who you are and aren't building for: plenty of our competitors are openly built for marketers for example, and while lots of marketers run all their reporting on PostHog (yours truly included), we're still building for AI-pilled engineers first, and we say so.
The reader who isn't a fit should leave feeling helped, not hustled. Honest pages also don't make enemies: the fastest way to go viral for the wrong reasons is a dodgy comparison, and if you'd rather not be bashed on Hacker News or Twitter for being slimy, be fair.
Take corrections from competitors.
We've shipped edits because someone at a competitor emailed us, DMed us, or better yet, opened a PR directly against our blog. We welcome it and encourage it. (Yes, if you're a competitor reading this, this is an invitation.)
Here's an example from today:
Lucas Harras, a Senior Customer Success Architect at Amplitude, read our PostHog vs Amplitude page, found four features we'd marked as missing that Amplitude actually has, and opened a PR.
We merged it the same day, and because every comparison table renders from that file (more on that below), every page that mentions any of these features was corrected by the next deploy.
Sometimes you'll be offered a slice of humble pie, and it's important to eat it gracefully.
My litmus test for every comparison: if a competitor wrote this exact page about PostHog, how would I feel reading it? Would it feel like they'd done their homework, or would I feel misrepresented and annoyed? If it's the latter, it's probably worth trying again.
We haven't always gotten this right. Part of it is that not everyone uses the same words for the same features, and some of our competitors have several hundred of them. A "sort of" column doesn't exist, so every row is ultimately a judgment call, and we've made some wrong ones.
But we're committed to doing better every time.
How to maintain comparison pages
Staying accurate across ~90 comparison and roundup pages for years is an engineering problem, and we started treating it like one.
1. Every competitor is a centralized data file.
In the posthog.com repo there's a folder with one file per competitor: sentry.tsx, amplitude.tsx, hotjar.tsx, and so on. Each file holds everything we claim about that company, in one place; here's a simplified version of what that looks like:
Feature keys come from a shared dictionary, so "session replay with network payloads" means the same thing on the Hotjar page as the LogRocket page.
Most of our comparison tables render from these files through one component. When a competitor ships a feature, someone changes one line in one file and every page that mentions them updates on the next deploy. The repo is public, so competitors can see exactly what we say about them and open a pull request if we're wrong.
2. Scouts checks our homework
Data files solve "update once, publish everywhere", but they don't solve for "notice that something changed" – that's what we've used Scouts for.
We run two. The first watches our competitors: it reads the competitor files I mentioned above, visits each competitor's pricing and docs pages, and reports back when what they say and what we say have drifted apart.
The second watches us. It turns out a very embarrassing way to get a comparison wrong isn't overstating a competitor, but understating yourself. (I learned this the hard way… occupational hazard of shipping as fast as we do. *wink*)
So the second scout reads our comparison pages against our own changelog, docs, open PRs, and Slack threads, and flags anywhere we might be underselling ourselves.
A few things make both of them better than a script that pings you every time a page changes:
- It has memory between runs, so it doesn't re-flag the same thing every week, and it learns what "normal" looks like for each site.
- It's selective by design. Most runs end with nothing to report, and that's it working. It ignores changes that don't affect the overall comparison.
- It shows its evidence: what their page says now, what our file says, and a suggested edit, with sources.
- A human ships the fix. The scout posts a digest to Slack with a link to open a PR. A person decides whether the change is necessary, opens the PR, and merges it.
Here's an example of what this looks like in practice. First, the Slack digest:
Then the full report in our self-driving inbox:
And finally, a pull request ready to merge:
The scout does the noticing, a human does the deciding, and nobody needs to add a recurring "re-read every competitor's pricing page" task to their calendar. Amen to that.
Where we go from here
We haven't reached our final form yet (will we ever?). One of my goals this quarter is going back through all of this content and making it better, and I'm sure there's plenty we're still getting wrong.
But the point is we started. Five years, 90-ish pages, and tens of thousands of signups later, "write honestly about the people trying to eat our lunch" has turned out to be one of the best decisions we've made for our organic content strategy; not the most intuitive one, but still one of the best.
So if you've been circling the plunge, take it. Be fair, be accurate, and let a robot handle the maintenance so you don't have to. (May I suggest ours?)
And if you're a peer who's nailed this (or who has failed at it and has war stories and words of caution to share), my DMs are always open.
PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

The second watches us. It turns out a very embarrassing way to get a comparison wrong isn't overstating a competitor, but understating yourself. (I learned this the hard way… occupational hazard of shipping as fast as we do. *wink*)
So the second scout reads our comparison pages against our own changelog, docs, open PRs, and Slack threads, and flags anywhere we might be underselling ourselves.
A few things make both of them better than a script that pings you every time a page changes:
- It has memory between runs, so it doesn't re-flag the same thing every week, and it learns what "normal" looks like for each site.
- It's selective by design. Most runs end with nothing to report, and that's it working. It ignores changes that don't affect the overall comparison.
- It shows its evidence: what their page says now, what our file says, and a suggested edit, with sources.
- A human ships the fix. The scout posts a digest to Slack with a link to open a PR. A person decides whether the change is necessary, opens the PR, and merges it.
Here's an example of what this looks like in practice. First, the Slack digest:
Then the full report in our self-driving inbox:
And finally, a pull request ready to merge:
The scout does the noticing, a human does the deciding, and nobody needs to add a recurring "re-read every competitor's pricing page" task to their calendar. Amen to that.
Where we go from here
We haven't reached our final form yet (will we ever?). One of my goals this quarter is going back through all of this content and making it better, and I'm sure there's plenty we're still getting wrong.
But the point is we started. Five years, 90-ish pages, and tens of thousands of signups later, "write honestly about the people trying to eat our lunch" has turned out to be one of the best decisions we've made for our organic content strategy; not the most intuitive one, but still one of the best.
So if you've been circling the plunge, take it. Be fair, be accurate, and let a robot handle the maintenance so you don't have to. (May I suggest ours?)
And if you're a peer who's nailed this (or who has failed at it and has war stories and words of caution to share), my DMs are always open.
PostHog is your product's context layer. With a full suite of developer tools – AI observability, product analytics, session replay, feature flags, experiments, error tracking, logs, and more – PostHog ingests and stores all the data agents need to diagnose problems, uncover opportunities, and ship fixes. A data warehouse and CDP tie it all together, unifying that context into one source agents can read across. You can steer it all from Slack, the web app, the desktop (PostHog Desktop), or your own editor via the MCP.

articles.title: Intel stock collapse worsens as $3.5T chip rout spreads
articles.body:
Wall Street mostly swept up last week's tech wreckage Monday. Chip stocks kept tracking mud back through the house.
About 7 in 10 S&P 500 stocks rose Monday, yet nearly every chip stock fell, and the group shed more than $400 billion in market value in a single session, by Yahoo Finance calculations.
Intel (INTC) led the way down again.
The chipmaker slid about 9% after its worst day since 1974 on Oct. 30, when a disappointing forecast knocked nearly 29% off the stock. Monday's close left Intel worth less than half of what it was when September ended.
And the damage didn't stick to Intel.
Micron (MU), Sandisk (SNDK), Seagate (STX), and Western Digital (WDC) — the memory and storage names that led the chip boom this year — all got clobbered, falling roughly 6% to 8%. Marvell (MRVL) fell even harder, a drop that came as it agreed to buy Lumentum (LITE) in a $115 billion deal. Nvidia (NVDA) held up better than most, but it's still down about 16% since Oct. 6.
Zoom out and the mess gets bigger. Chip and memory stocks have lost about $3.7 trillion in market value since Oct. 6, by Yahoo Finance calculations. Nvidia lost the most in dollars, but Intel's drop of nearly half is the steepest among the giants.
Not everything tied to AI bled. SpaceX (SPCX) rose, though it's still well below where it started October. Software was mixed, apart from cybersecurity stocks like Fortinet (FTNT) and CrowdStrike (CRWD), which fell with chips.
Adam Johnson, founder of the Bullseye Brief and portfolio manager of the American Ingenuity Fund, thinks last week's sell-off already priced in the worst.
"The market kitchen-sinked it," Johnson told Yahoo Finance on Monday. "They discounted everything that could go wrong. And when you do that, typically that's when you see a bottom."
John Chambers, founder and CEO of JC2 Ventures and Cisco's former CEO, expects the gap between winners and losers to keep widening.
"There will be major train wrecks," Chambers told Yahoo Finance, also on Monday. "And rising tide does not raise all boats. I would not bet against Nvidia."
Stock Trader's Almanac editor Jeff Hirsch, who coined the term "Octoberphobia," bought the sell-off on Oct. 30. History is on his side. Chips have climbed in all eight midterm cycles since 1994, measured from the last October close through the following June, by Yahoo Finance calculations. But in 2002 and 2018, they first fell about another 11%.
Next up is AMD (AMD), which reports third quarter results Tuesday after the bell, the same day as the midterm vote.
