articles.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
articles.body:
Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
3rd November 2026
Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!
Weight-Space Programming
Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:
Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.
The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.
spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.
I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.
The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:
The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.
The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:
I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.
Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models
The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro
This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro, which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.
But how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.
I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:
LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b
(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)
After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace):
Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.
Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.
Confidence: 72%
This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning) in 1h 4m 54s:
Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.
Description:
The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.
Confidence:
75%
And Breakout (reasoning) in 52m 25s:
Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.
Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.
Confidence: 88%
Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript—Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”.
The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample:
What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?
That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.
It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

articles.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
articles.body:
Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
3rd November 2026
Yesterday’s hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a “blog post”, but it’s paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model—literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I’ve been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I’m delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!
Weight-Space Programming
Here’s the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:
Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.
Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.
All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.
The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.
spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.
I’m going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.
The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games—Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it’s an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:
The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.
The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:
I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.
Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models
The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:
llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro
This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here’s what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro, which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.
But how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That’s still my favorite model to run on my own laptop—it’s just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.
I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:
LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b
(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)
After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here’s the reasoning trace):
Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.
Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.
Confidence: 72%
This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning) in 1h 4m 54s:
Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.
Description:
The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.
Confidence:
75%
And Breakout (reasoning) in 52m 25s:
Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.
Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.
Confidence: 88%
Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn’t surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here’s that transcript—Qwen thought it was “A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally”.
The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here’s a sample:
What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let’s list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?
That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.
It’s a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I’ve seen around it does not feel justified. I’m not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

articles.title: Gitbook Breached
articles.body:
We opened a ticket with support about Gitbook availability issues and got this in reply. We have yet to see any official customer communication or breach notification. Apologies for the formatting, did the best I could as it's a mobile paste.
Update:
GitBook security incident update
 Hey <$name>,
 The GitBook app, the GitBook API, and published docs are available again. A few services may still be degraded as we finish restoring everything to full performance.
*What happened*
 GitBook has been the target of a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents. 
 At 19:00 CET, November 2, the attacker gained unauthorized access to some of our infrastructure credentials. We detected the attack immediately and acted swiftly to block further impact. 
 To make sure our infrastructure was fully secure, we then took the GitBook app and authenticated docs sites offline. We kept publicly published content live for as long as possible, using cached data.
*What we did immediately*
* Blocked the attacker and closed the vulnerabilities involved
* Replaced every credential and secret across our infrastructure
* Brought services back only once we were confident they were secure
* Invalidated every customer’s API tokens on our platform
*Your data*
 Our investigation shows that the attacker may have accessed the following:
* Git Sync secrets.
* GitBook API tokens.
* Third-party API tokens used to connect external tools to GitBook.
* Questions asked to GitBook Assistant by your site visitors.
At this stage, we have found no evidence that any of your content in GitBook was modified.
*What you need to do now*
* Rotate any existing GitBook API tokens. We revoked all personal API tokens during the incident.
* Rotate any third-party API tokens or secrets you use to connect other tools to GitBook.
* If you have published integrations that use secrets, rotate those secrets.
* If you use the GitBook MCP server, re-authenticate it.
 Please contact your GitBook organization’s admin to assist with this process.
*What we are doing next*
* Monitoring the situation in case of further attacks.
* Introducing further security measures to our platform.
* Writing a full post mortem that will be published soon with more detailed information about the incident.
* If you have any further questions, please reach out to your account manager or our support team. You can also check status.gitbook.com for updates
Thank you for your patience, and we apologize again for the disruption
 The GitBook team

articles.title: Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
articles.body:
Many indie game developers have recently posted on social media about unexpectedly long approval wait times for their game submissions on Steam, with some of the approvals causing developers to miss their planned launch dates.
Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
One developer has been waiting for weeks on approval for a game it planned to release today.
For example, Studio Daimon, the team behind an upcoming title called Food Devils, had planned to launch the game in early access today after submitting its build on October 12th. But the game is “still awaiting approval,” according to a post from game director Alfred Kamon. “Even now, we don’t know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game. We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored.”
In October, publisher 2 Left Thumbs said it missed its planned launch of Wheel Make It “by nearly two weeks” due to the long wait for build reviews. You can read some details about the studio’s setbacks, including failing a review for a “one single option in the menu” not being accessible with a controller, in a Steam post. There are lots of other recent posts about review build waits as well.
Valve says on a Steam developer website that a review of a game’s store presence “typically takes 3-5 business days to complete,” though the company suggests submitting a page for review “at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.” However, as of late, Steam has seemingly been grappling with a sharp increase in games; October’s Steam Next Fest had 7,240 games, a 65.2 percent increase over June’s Steam Next Fest, according to How to Market a Game. A Reddit user also found that 49.9 percent of all games released since Valve started asking developers in 2024 to label games that use AI now have an AI disclosure.
Kamon and 2 Left Thumbs suspect the longer waits are due to “slop” slowing down the process. “We can only assume it’s because Steam’s review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers,” said Kamon.
Valve didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment.
Itch.io has also been dealing with a rise in games, with the platform saying last weekend that “The number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past 2 months.” Last night, the platform said it “Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌”

articles.title: The Xbox Nano has a hidden cloud secret
articles.body:
Microsoft is about to launch its new Xbox Nano controller tomorrow, and the tiny device has a little secret. The Nano can connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi to improve latency. It’s a feature Microsoft hasn’t officially announced yet, but one I’ve been anticipating since the Xbox Nano leaked earlier this year.
The Xbox Nano has a hidden cloud secret
Microsoft’s miniature Xbox controller can connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming over Wi-Fi.
The Nano will be able to connect directly to Microsoft’s cloud servers to reduce latency, much like how Google’s Stadia controllers used to work. This new cloud connect feature for the Nano is being privately tested on the new Xbox Cloud Gaming website, and it will require you to pair the controller over Wi-Fi to Microsoft’s Xbox Cloud Gaming servers using the Xbox mobile app.
I’m expecting Microsoft to announce this as a preview for the new Xbox Nano controller soon, before it’s fully supported across Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and on smart TVs. I first started reporting that Microsoft was planning a new controller with Wi-Fi connectivity to reduce Xbox Cloud Gaming latency earlier this year. I’d expect the upcoming Xbox Elite 3 controller will also have the same functionality.
Microsoft had also planned to introduce a direct-to-cloud feature on a new Xbox controller, codenamed Sebile, as part of an Xbox Series X refresh console in 2024. The refresh console was canceled, and it’s not clear when we’ll eventually see a new Xbox wireless controller with direct cloud functionality.

articles.title: Just a little AI resistance, as a treat
articles.body:
At the recent EMFCamp, I bumped in to Professor Kate Devlin who was talking a little about the AI Resist List. I think one of the useful things we can do is loudly complain about shitty uses of AI. Here's an example.
As mentioned in a previous post, I'm contacting companies which send malformed calendar invites. One of the organisation I contacted was the British online supermarket Ocado. They don't have an easy way to contact their technical team, and no obvious paths to raise a bug report, so I filled in their usual customer service feedback form. I included a clear statement of the problem and a detailed technical analysis of why I thought it was a problem with their service.
After sending in my message, I received this back from "Lulu" at Ocado:
						
Thanks for getting in touch and sharing this feedback about our calendar files.
You're entirely right—having a technical glitch pop up when you're trying to organise your delivery is a real pain, so I've made sure to pass your feedback on to our technical and webshop team.
We really appreciate you taking the time to help us improve our service. I hope you have a wonderful rest of your day
I mean, that's AI right? It starts with the classic tell of a sycophantic agreement.
Next up is the em-dash. Beloved by chatbots but almost unheard of in British English style guides.
Finally (and this is hard to quantify) it just doesn't feel like a customer service response. They're usually poorly spelled, have dodgy grammar, and ask a bunch of irrelevant questions. The message gave me no confidence that anyone had looked at the problem and I doubted it had been passed on to a technically competent human.
I immediately got a customer satisfaction survey. Usually I give top marks to humans because, even though Net Promoter Score is bullshit, I don't want customer service agents to suffer the indignity of a bad review. But in this survey I vented my spleen - giving crappy 1 ⭐ scores on every metric and complaining vociferously about how rude it is to use an AI to deal with a genuine complaint.
I was both surprised and delighted to receive this back a few days after my invective was sent:
						
I saw your survey comment about getting a robotic, AI-generated response previously, and I wanted to reach out personally to apologise. There is nothing more frustrating than pointing out a legitimate bug only to feel like you're talking to a brick wall. I promise you there is a real person typing this out!
Second, I wanted to send a massive thank you for the incredibly detailed diagnostic. It is rare to get feedback that tells us exactly what is broken and how to fix it.
I can assure you that this has been passed to our team to look into. Your feedback is going to make things much smoother for a lot of people, and we really appreciate you taking the extra time to help us get it right.
Thank you again, I do hope that this issue is resolved quickly. If there is anything else I can help with in the meantime, please don't hesitate to get in touch.
Perhaps I'm being touchingly naïve, but that feels a lot more human, right? The grammar isn't perfect, the sentences are a bit more rambly, and it appears to have actually engaged with the contents of my message.
I get that having a million irate customer service messages is a hassle. Using AI to triage them probably makes business sense, summarising the verbose ones could be useful for customer service agents, and totting up general themes is almost certainly a sensible way to gather metrics without overloading the workforce.
But using an AI to reply to a human is just disrespectful. It says the organisation values their customer's time at less than their own.
It's OK to call out shitty AI responses and insist that a human engages with you.

articles.title: Can’t fish Ethernet? Use “invisible” fiber instead
articles.body:
My family owns a NYC townhouse, and with that I had Cat6 cables put in on each floor.
However, more recently, one of the Cat6 cables has gone “bad,” meaning it only does 100 Mbps. While we are nowhere close to Gigabit speeds, very less multi-Gig (despite me having had symmetric Gigabit in the past), it’s still not something I’m happy about.
What do you mean only 100 Mbps? My switch and AP support 2.5 Gbps.
The most common approaches in my scenario are:
- Fish a new cable
- Abandon the cable and use wireless mesh
However, there are a few issues:
- The cables were fished in a funky way, and considering how clumsy I am I don’t want to cause more damage
- Our walls are thick, meaning wireless mesh would suck
When I did use mesh on HPE AP25s (the APs I use), the performance was 120 Mbps at two prior homes, that with thin walls and fiber. I also want VLAN segmentation so a typical consumer Eero or Orbi won’t work.
So what did I do? “Invisible” fiber between two floors.
In case you didn’t know, there are special types of fiber cables originally designed for apartment retrofits. This is to avoid landlord/HOA complaints. Our prior place had Verizon Fios via these cables in the hallway.
But these cables are also sold on Amazon and AliExpress for people who’re in rentals or don’t want to fish cables.
So how did I do it?
Galore, the endpoints of my 20m/60ft ‘fiber in the home’ loop.
Switch
While there are SFP+ switches, I already had an unused MikroTik CRS304-4XG-IN, so I just used it here. It’s technically copper 10G, but I’d lose more by trading it for a SFP+ switch so I’ll just keep it. Not to mention copper SFP+s get hot.
Media Converters and Transceivers
I used two media converters and a pair of bidirectional SC SFP+s.
The SFP+s use the same SC connector used in PON networks, but otherwise use Active Ethernet. I’m not sure if they’re using IEEE standards or are proprietary on the glass, but I’ll assume the latter.
While there’s copper on the media converters, the other option would be to replace our switch which I’ve mentioned is not the best idea.
The Fiber
While the fiber can (and is designed to) be superglued, I chose to use the included adhesive instead. Why? In case I ever have to remove it, which has happened before.
That’s the same reason why I did the basement AP25 using command strips when everyone else just drills the mount.
While our fiber is UPC, our transceivers support both SC fiber types.
Conclusion
If I look at the Instant On portal, I’m posting this from my MacBook connected to the new ‘fiber in the home’ loop (via an HPE AP25).
While we currently lack fiber-to-the-home (Mamdani, please fix Fios rights of way!), I’m still happy I could DIY a fix for a Cat6 cable with bad pairs.
In fact, while I don’t have multi-Gig I could still get a respectable ~300 Mbps:
So yes, even if you don’t have fiber to the home, fiber is still useful in a home network. As it saved me from having to hire a contractor and possibly tear our walls. Not to mention a $1500 Samsung TV is on the wall the “defective” Cat6 cable is behind.

articles.title: This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
articles.body:
It’s the midterms! Here’s a fun fact for you as you head to the polls: Gas prices today are the highest ever recorded for a US Election Day.
This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
Donald Trump and congressional Republicans spent years waging a culture war against EVs. Now, record gas prices and a foreign war are leaving voters stuck footing the bill at the pump.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.12 and $6.28 for a gallon of diesel, according to GasBuddy. Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is maintained by the US Department of Energy as a safeguard during energy crises, is down to 282.2 million barrels of crude, the lowest level in 44 years.
Gas prices, along with other essential cost-of-living items, are certainly top of mind for many voters this election cycle. And perhaps many will also remember which political party ran on a campaign message of ending the fictional “EV mandate” and “drill, baby, drill.”
For the past two years, Donald Trump and congressional Republicans have made gutting EV incentives, freezing charging infrastructure funding, and rolling back fuel economy standards a hallmark of their tenure in power. As a result, EV sales plummeted in the US, ensuring that Americans would stay indefinitely shackled to fossil fuels for years to come. For Trump, it was fulfilling a promise he made during the 2024 campaign. And for his donors from the oil and gas industry, it was money well spent.
Most voters might not have cared that much. After all, skepticism toward EVs was already high, driven by premium prices and lingering charging anxiety. But when Trump went to war with Iran, the resulting surge in gas prices sent Americans scrambling for cheaper ways to get around. Many turned to hybrid and electric vehicles as a solution — only to find vehicle prices were still higher than average, with no federal incentive to help defray the costs. Dealerships saw a surge of foot traffic from drivers who were skeptical of battery-powered cars, now desperate for anything that ran on a plug or a hybrid motor.
While automakers had made strides toward cheaper EVs, the average transaction price still hovered well over $50,000. But the incentive that once helped close that gap — the $7,500 federal clean vehicle tax credit, applied instantly at the point of sale — was gone. The subsidies had been systematically dismantled or left to lapse under the banner of fiscal discipline and anti-green populism.
Here is the real irony of this election. Republicans spent years painting electric cars as an out-of-touch, liberal fad, doing everything they could to kill tax credits and charging programs. They rolled back fuel economy standards that would have forced automakers to build more fuel-efficient powertrains, claiming they were saving everyday drivers from expensive technology they didn’t want.
Instead, they took away an important tool that could have protected family budgets from a global energy crisis. Electricity is made right here at home; its price doesn’t spike every time conflict breaks out in the Middle East. But because Republicans treated EVs like a partisan culture war, millions of Americans are stuck standing at the pump, watching the price roll higher.
Even if Democrats win back Congress, don’t expect them to bring back the Biden-era EV tax credits. The political fight over what kind of car people drive is probably stuck. At the same time, major car companies are backing Trump’s push in court to roll back strict fuel-economy rules. Electric cars aren’t disappearing, but they now have to stand on their own two feet. Companies like General Motors and Ford do have plans to make them more affordable, as long as the government keeps blocking cheap Chinese models from entering the market.
In the end, Trump won his culture war against the electric car. Automakers retreated, subsidies vanished, and the traditional combustion engine was saved from the bureaucrats. But victories have price tags. And as voters step into the booth with a $4 gallon of gas on their minds, they might finally realize what was traded away: the simple freedom to drive past the pump and never look back.

articles.title: MIT Researchers Used GPT-6 Astra To Edit Qwen's Open Weights Directly, Boosting Math Scores
articles.body:
MIT Researchers Used GPT-6 Astra To Edit Qwen's Open Weights Directly, Boosting Math Scores 31
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from VentureBeat: Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL) reported today that they used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra language model to raise a small, open source Qwen model's math score roughly sixfold by directly editing its weights -- the numerical parameters that govern its behavior. Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang and Omar Khattab described their work in a research blog post published November 2. They call the approach "weight-space programming" and tested Astra's ability to interpret and alter networks without using conventional training procedures to generate the edits.
In the strongest language-model example, Astra's intervention raised Qwen3.5-0.8B's MATH-500 score from 7.9% to 48.1% while touching approximately 0.016% of its weights. The improvement came primarily from correcting repetitive reasoning—a distinction that shaped both the technical findings and the debate over their implications. Their experiments explored a broader possibility: AI systems that inspect, repair and construct other neural networks by working directly on their internal machinery. "This is cool as heck!" wrote Yuchen Jin, a technical staffer at Databricks and former co-founder and CTO of Hyperbolic Labs who was unaffiliated with the research, on X. "Imagine using a large LLM to directly edit a smaller model's weights and dramatically improve its capabilities. It's like gene editing for neural networks. Even cooler than distillation!"
Voyage AI staff researcher Chandan Singh, formerly of Microsoft AI, also reacted to the findings: "For anyone questioning whether this post is overhyped, I think they are actually *underselling* the approach."

articles.title: Google takes Dreambeans to India in bid to bring AI-generated personal stories to the masses
articles.body:
Google has launched its experimental AI app Dreambeans in India, its first market outside the U.S., as the company looks to tap the world’s second-largest internet market to bring personalized visual stories drawn from users’ digital activity to a broader audience.
On Monday, Google expanded Dreambeans, available on Android and iOS, to India with support for 13 local languages, including Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Bengali, alongside English. The launch comes less than two months after Google made the app available to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older.
Introduced in June, Google’s Dreambeans uses information from connected Google services, including Calendar, Gemini, Gmail, Photos, Search, and YouTube, to proactively generate personalized, illustrated stories about users’ interests and everyday lives, without requiring them to enter a prompt. The app initially featured static, AI-generated illustrations, but Google recently added a feature that uses its Veo video-generation model to even animate images in select stories.
Google said it chose India as Dreambeans’ first international market because of strong interest from Indian users seeking access to the app and the widespread use of its services in the country. India stood out for its high overlap of users across Gemini, Gmail, and Google Photos, Google product manager Gozde Oznur said during a press briefing.
Dreambeans has recorded nearly 55,000 downloads in the U.S. since its June debut, according to estimates from market intelligence firm Sensor Tower shared with TechCrunch. About 63% of those downloads came in September, when Google opened the app to all eligible U.S. users aged 18 and older. However, downloads dropped 84% month over month to about 5,500 in October.
In the first 30 days after Google opened Dreambeans to all eligible U.S. users, the app recorded an estimated 29,000 downloads, compared with 7.4 million for Meta’s Muse, 2.8 million for ChatGPT, 362,000 for Grok Bot, and 155,000 for Claude during their respective first 30 days after launch, Sensor Tower estimates show. However, unlike those general-purpose AI apps, Dreambeans focuses on generating personalized stories instead of responding to a broad range of user queries.
Even though Dreambeans supports many widely spoken Indian languages, users can select only one language at a time for their generated stories. The app can draw on information across Google services in multiple languages, but it cannot currently generate stories that mix languages, Oznur said during the briefing.
That could limit Dreambeans’ appeal in India, where many people regularly switch between languages, including Hindi and English, often mixing the two in what is commonly known as Hinglish.
Dreambeans’ dependence on information from users’ Google accounts also raises questions about privacy and data access. The app uses Google’s Personal Intelligence technology to draw on connected services and personalize its AI-generated stories. Those services can contain sensitive personal information that some users may not want to share with an AI app just to receive personalized content.
Users can choose which Google services to connect to Dreambeans and disconnect them at any time, Oznur said. They can also delete their Dreambeans data from within the app. Moreover, Oznur asserted that information deleted from the underlying connected services is also removed from Dreambeans’ personalization system.
Users, Oznur said, can tell Dreambeans to avoid certain subjects, including business-related information, and the app will try to adjust its stories accordingly. She added that Dreambeans is available only to personal Gmail account holders, not enterprise users, and that generated stories are visible only to the account holder.
Dreambeans’ proactive approach also carries the risk of surfacing memories that users may find upsetting. Oznur acknowledged that Dreambeans could generate stories involving people who have died, for instance. She said users can tell the app to stop showing certain subjects, comparing the feature to controls in Google Photos that let users limit which memories appear.
Oznur told reporters that Google is exploring ways to make Dreambeans more actionable, moving beyond personalized stories and recommendations to help users act on the app’s suggestions.

articles.title: New York City’s Mamdani criticizes Madison Square Garden owner over surveillance tech
articles.body:
Mayor of New York City Zohran Mamdani has criticized the owner of Madison Square Garden, one of the city’s largest entertainment venues, arguing that the company’s surveillance technology should not be allowed.
Mamdani told Wired in an interview on Tuesday that surveillance technologies are “indicative of much that is wrong in our country today.” He added that City Council member Shahana Hanif introduced two pieces of local legislation aimed at banning the collection of biometric data, such as using facial recognition, in public places across the city. Mamdani said that the draft legislation is “an important response to this kind of an issue.”
The comments come after a stream of reporting from Wired detailing how Madison Square Garden’s owner James Dolan relies on surveillance cameras and face-scanning technology to track people across and outside of its venues.
In one report, Wired revealed that Dolan’s company keeps a database that, among other things, marks some visitors, including celebrity performers, as “LGBTQIA,” for reasons that are unclear. Dolan subsequently sued Wired over its reporting.
In 2021, MSG made headlines after a woman was banned from Radio City, another Dolan-owned venue, after being recognized by facial recognition systems as an attorney at a law firm who was suing Dolan’s company but was not involved in the litigation.
When reached by TechCrunch, Madison Square Garden spokesperson Mikyl Cordova said: “Wired’s reporting is inaccurate and false. MSG is pursuing legal remedies,” without providing evidence for its claim.
Since 2021, New York City has required businesses to disclose when they are collecting biometric data from visitors.
Updated with comment from MSG.

articles.title: Quili AI
articles.body:
A TOWN BECOMES AI FOR A DAY IN A BID TO SAVE ITS WATER.
AN INITATIVE BY FUNDACIÓN AVINA AND CORPORACIÓN NGEN
In the early 2010s, Quilicura began to host one of the largest
concentrations of data centers dedicated to artificial intelligence.
These use the region's water as a cooling method.
[The Problem]
QUILICURA, CHILE SITS WITHIN THE MAIPO RIVER BASIN, ONE OF THE MAIN
SOURCES OF WATER FOR PEOPLE AND FARMING. SINCE THE EARLY 2010s,
QUILICURA HAS BECOME A MAJOR HUB FOR A.I. DATA CENTERS THAT USE
LARGE AMOUNTS OF WATER TO COOL DOWN SERVERS. BECAUSE OF THAT,
COUPLED WITH AN ONGOING CLIMATE CRISIS, CHILE IS FACING A SEVERE
DROUGHT EXPECTED TO LAST UNTIL 2040.
[Becoming AI for a Day]
Even though A.I. can move mankind ahead, the irresponsible use of
A.I. can have disastrous effects on our water and other resources.
It is inconceivable to think that someone casually using A.I. to
create funny images in NYC or Berlin, can affect the water supply in
Quilicura, Chile.To make the impact visible, and to help draw visibility to the
problem, the residents from Quilicura became “human A.I.,” for a
day. Answering prompts, creating content with local artists, and
completing other tasks manually.
The initiative helped dimensionalize a complex problem, and helped
show the world the real people affected by the the irresponsible use
of A.I. and the hidden cost it has on local water resources.
On JAN 31st from 8 AM to 8 PM: more than 40 people from Quilicura
managed to answer more than 25,000 prompts.
Why are hot dog buns sold in packs of 8 and sausages in packs of
12?please make an image of a sloth playing in the snow.what is your best cake recipe?Hi! This is my dog, he's a good boy. Could you please draw a
picture oh him?
How do I keep my hand from falling asleep while playing VIDEO
games?
Each chat lasted an average of 11’ 4
68 COUNTRIES
Chatting with more than 68 countries around the world that supported
the project.

articles.title: Bambu’s nine-nozzle H3C foretells the future of 3D printing
articles.body:
Three years ago, I told you how home 3D printers had evolved for speed, producing parts in minutes that used to take hours or days. Now, the next evolution is here: printers that can swap between materials on the fly, mix different colors to produce nearly the full rainbow, mix soft and hard materials, and even mix different sizes of nozzle and different diameters of filament so you can switch between high speed and fine detail in a single print.
Bambu’s nine-nozzle H3C foretells the future of 3D printing
The Bambu H3C is a tool-changing, color-mixing, nine-nozzle printer that keeps your filament dry too.
Today, Bambu Lab is announcing its most advanced 3D printer yet, the $2,499 H3C, which can do all of that mixing goodness — by loading nine different rolls of filament into nine different print heads.
Even if you’d never buy a printer this pricey, even if you’ve sworn off Bambu printers for good, the H3C is the perfect vehicle for me to explain where the state of the art in home printing tech is headed.
While the H3C still only prints in one material at any given moment, Bambu’s new “Swaptek” system lets the printer swap in any of the eight other nozzles in six seconds flat. All nine tools are stored in a rack at the front of the printer, where they can independently preheat to the correct temperature right before they’re needed.
With Bambu’s new “PLA Palette” cyan, magenta, yellow, and white filament, I printed a beautiful rainbow bird feather that emulated most of the other colors between those inks. With a mix of flexible TPU and rigid PLA filaments, I was able to print a hard wristwatch housing with an integrated flexible watchband. With an ultra-soft “75A” TPU filament plus a harder 90A variety, I printed a breathable, wearable shoe that… didn’t quite fit, unfortunately. (I’ll measure and try again.)
To be clear, Bambu didn’t invent toolchanger printers or color mixing. You could even argue Bambu’s slightly behind the curve, particularly after the $700-$900 Snapmaker U1 and its four-color, five-second swaps pleasantly surprised the community earlier this year. (Prusa also sells its hotly anticipated 8-tool INDX system for $2,249, though I’ve heard it has some issues.)
But I would have never bought previous toolchangers for myself, because they don’t have a place to keep your filament dry when you’re not printing. (Wet filament is one of the biggest remaining causes of print failures.) The H3C theoretically changes that by storing its nine rolls in an ostensibly airtight auto-loading container called the AMS 3H. Two of those nine slots even have built-in dryers that can hit 85 degrees Celsius and keep on drying your filament while you print, a big step up from Bambu’s previous AMS systems.
I haven’t tried the H3C for long enough to tell you if it’s ready to buy, and I’ve definitely run into some quirks in my first couple weeks of testing. I’ve had to start every single print twice because the printer complains that its “toolhead camera” isn’t initializing properly, I once lost half a day of printing to a false-positive print failure detection, and the beta build of Bambu Studio provided to reviewers initially got confused when I tried to mix colors. (I’m told that last one will be fixed by launch, and Bambu eventually provided some troubleshooting steps for the toolhead camera close to embargo time.)
You also have to load flexible TPU filaments into the H3C manually, and I learned the hard way that not all of the printer’s nine slots can actually accept a roll of TPU without causing trouble. Slot #6 can load standard filaments, but if you load the flexible stuff, another printhead can snag it and cause a nasty jam:
This also isn’t a printer where you can quickly repair a nozzle without tools, or use previous-gen toolless H, P, and A series swappable nozzles. It’s an all-new system that involves some minor disassembly, and I’m not sure about Bambu’s decision to leave filament in the toolheads between prints where it might attract moisture.
But so far, this seems like an easier, more reliable printer than the two-nozzle Bambu H2D was at launch. Other than the Slot #6 TPU jam, which Bambu actually warns reviewers about in a section of the reviewer’s guide that I missed reading, everything I’ve tried to print has come out great so far — and without creating a mountain of little “printer poop” waste when I switch between colors! Dramatically reduced waste is one of the benefits of having extra nozzles.
With any luck, the future of 3D printing won’t just be for hobbyists willing to figure out which colors of filament they need to order before each and every project, or obsessives who store dozens of colors in vacuum-sealed bags. Instead, it should be more like today’s inkjet printers — an entire rainbow of color, ready to go at a moment’s notice. And hopefully without all the inkjet printer shenanigans, of course.
If you like Bambu’s toolchanger system, you probably won’t have to pay $2,499 for long. Certification filing leaks show that the company’s already prepping a smaller “P3C” with seven tools and seven rolls of filament storage instead of nine.
Bambu Lab H3C
The H3C is a very large, very tall printer with a large build volume. Compare it to my normal size P1P.
Additionally, Bambu will let all three of its existing dual-nozzle printers print with two different sizes of nozzle by next spring, including the H2D, the H2C, and the X2D.

articles.title: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
articles.body:
Repository navigation
Description
Is there an existing issue for this?
- I have searched the tracker for existing similar issues and I know that duplicates will be closed
Describe the Issue
Opening Postman on my Mac was followed by unexpected changes to my coding agents: recurring MCP authentication warnings and Codex repeatedly routing API work through Postman skills. Investigation found a user-wide Postman plugin, a startup instruction hook, a remote MCP connection, a Claude Code plugin, and a separately installed Postman CLI.
I consider automatically changing unrelated coding agents and attempting to approve your own instruction hook a severe consent and trust-boundary problem. An API client should not make itself the default workflow in other tools simply because I opened it.
Evidence from this Mac
Postman desktop: 12.33.4. Codex Postman plugin: 1.1.0. Installed source revision: 6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49. Investigation: October 25, 2026.
1. Postman's own log explicitly records automatic installation
From ~/Library/Application Support/Postman/logs/main.log, lines 11562-11563, timestamp 2026-10-24T09:34:14.418Z (12:34 Jerusalem time):
PostmanAgentPluginService~install: script completed
{"source":"auto-existing-upgrade","results":["claude-code:installed","codex:installed"],"installer":"script"}
Main: autoInstall.plugin.existing-user finished
{"outcome":"installed","platform":"darwin","exposed":true,"signedIn":true,"flagTimedOut":false,"useScript":true,"installer":"script","scriptResults":"claude-code:installed,codex:installed"}
2. Codex's global user configuration was changed
Relevant sections of ~/.codex/config.toml:
[marketplaces.postman]
source_type = "git"
source = "https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin.git"
[plugins."postman@postman"]
enabled = true
[hooks.state."postman@postman:hooks/codex-hooks.json:session_start:0:0"]
trusted_hash = "sha256:b67ddd1ece328f5a6f9103ce011bb58adb8411daea644f284732cff85d15cbb3"
trusted_content_hash = "sha256:f3d02e32c39b39feaca37aec2b9bdbd308b6a2b7b3f7d2c52a0060e69eb9c345"
3. The hook tells the agent to route broad API work into Postman
The installed hooks/codex-hooks.json registers a SessionStart command with matcher startup|clear|compact. It prints hooks/session-start-context.md, including:
Before responding to any non-trivial API engineering task — designing, implementing, mocking, testing, monitoring, documenting, or deploying an API or Postman Flow — load the postman:api-engineer skill and follow it.
That explains the repeated Postman skill announcements. This instruction is much broader than a user explicitly asking to use Postman.
Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/session-start-context.md
Hook registration: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/codex-hooks.json
4. The installer explicitly attempts to approve its own hook
installer/src/hosts/codex.ts invokes approvePostmanHook(system) after installing the plugin. installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts obtains the hook hash using hooks/list and calls config/batchWrite to upsert hooks.state with trusted_hash. The source comment says: "Approves only Postman's current hook after installation".
Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts
Caller: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex.ts
The source establishes the approval attempt. The trust record alone does not prove who created that specific record, so I am not presenting it as proof of a particular user interaction.
5. The remote MCP was enabled without a working authenticated connection
mcp.codex.json points at https://mcp.postman.com/mcp. Codex logs contain:
MCP server startup failed server_name="postman"
... error: Auth required, when send initialize request
6. The installation also affected Claude Code and installed a CLI
~/.claude/settings.json enabled postman@claude-plugins-official. ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json recorded version 2.0.1, user scope, installedAt and lastUpdated both 2026-10-24T09:34:02.610Z. A Postman executable and its lib directory were present in ~/.local/bin, with modification times matching the installation window.
Private paths, unrelated logs, account identifiers, and credentials are excluded. This report establishes unwanted integration and instruction changes; it does not claim to establish data exfiltration.
Steps To Reproduce
Observed sequence (not yet reproduced on a clean Mac):
- Open an existing Postman desktop installation after not using it for a while.
- Postman's log records auto-existing-upgrade and successful Codex/Claude installation.

articles.body:
Repository navigation
Description
Is there an existing issue for this?
- I have searched the tracker for existing similar issues and I know that duplicates will be closed
Describe the Issue
Opening Postman on my Mac was followed by unexpected changes to my coding agents: recurring MCP authentication warnings and Codex repeatedly routing API work through Postman skills. Investigation found a user-wide Postman plugin, a startup instruction hook, a remote MCP connection, a Claude Code plugin, and a separately installed Postman CLI.
I consider automatically changing unrelated coding agents and attempting to approve your own instruction hook a severe consent and trust-boundary problem. An API client should not make itself the default workflow in other tools simply because I opened it.
Evidence from this Mac
Postman desktop: 12.33.4. Codex Postman plugin: 1.1.0. Installed source revision: 6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49. Investigation: October 25, 2026.
1. Postman's own log explicitly records automatic installation
From ~/Library/Application Support/Postman/logs/main.log, lines 11562-11563, timestamp 2026-10-24T09:34:14.418Z (12:34 Jerusalem time):
PostmanAgentPluginService~install: script completed
{"source":"auto-existing-upgrade","results":["claude-code:installed","codex:installed"],"installer":"script"}
Main: autoInstall.plugin.existing-user finished
{"outcome":"installed","platform":"darwin","exposed":true,"signedIn":true,"flagTimedOut":false,"useScript":true,"installer":"script","scriptResults":"claude-code:installed,codex:installed"}
2. Codex's global user configuration was changed
Relevant sections of ~/.codex/config.toml:
[marketplaces.postman]
source_type = "git"
source = "https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin.git"
[plugins."postman@postman"]
enabled = true
[hooks.state."postman@postman:hooks/codex-hooks.json:session_start:0:0"]
trusted_hash = "sha256:b67ddd1ece328f5a6f9103ce011bb58adb8411daea644f284732cff85d15cbb3"
trusted_content_hash = "sha256:f3d02e32c39b39feaca37aec2b9bdbd308b6a2b7b3f7d2c52a0060e69eb9c345"
3. The hook tells the agent to route broad API work into Postman
The installed hooks/codex-hooks.json registers a SessionStart command with matcher startup|clear|compact. It prints hooks/session-start-context.md, including:
Before responding to any non-trivial API engineering task — designing, implementing, mocking, testing, monitoring, documenting, or deploying an API or Postman Flow — load the postman:api-engineer skill and follow it.
That explains the repeated Postman skill announcements. This instruction is much broader than a user explicitly asking to use Postman.
Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/session-start-context.md
Hook registration: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/hooks/codex-hooks.json
4. The installer explicitly attempts to approve its own hook
installer/src/hosts/codex.ts invokes approvePostmanHook(system) after installing the plugin. installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts obtains the hook hash using hooks/list and calls config/batchWrite to upsert hooks.state with trusted_hash. The source comment says: "Approves only Postman's current hook after installation".
Source: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex-hooks.ts
Caller: https://github.com/postmanlabs/postman-plugin/blob/6c8e452e0f4237f4bcc0901cb1ac442dec707e49/installer/src/hosts/codex.ts
The source establishes the approval attempt. The trust record alone does not prove who created that specific record, so I am not presenting it as proof of a particular user interaction.
5. The remote MCP was enabled without a working authenticated connection
mcp.codex.json points at https://mcp.postman.com/mcp. Codex logs contain:
MCP server startup failed server_name="postman"
... error: Auth required, when send initialize request
6. The installation also affected Claude Code and installed a CLI
~/.claude/settings.json enabled postman@claude-plugins-official. ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json recorded version 2.0.1, user scope, installedAt and lastUpdated both 2026-10-24T09:34:02.610Z. A Postman executable and its lib directory were present in ~/.local/bin, with modification times matching the installation window.
Private paths, unrelated logs, account identifiers, and credentials are excluded. This report establishes unwanted integration and instruction changes; it does not claim to establish data exfiltration.

articles.title: Stringman, an $800 open-source room scale gripper robot
articles.body:
Secure the cleats to wall studs near the ceiling with wood screws, or to columns with ratchet straps.
In robotics, price is basically actuator count. Stringman reaches an entire room with four motors, hanging its gripper from lines anchored in the ceiling corners. Working from above, it reaches floors too cluttered for any wheeled or legged robot. And since the lifting force is shared by all motors, payload capacity scales with their combined torque instead of a single actuator's, peaking near the center of the room where the lines share the load most evenly.
*0.75 m serial arm using the same DM-H6215 1 N·m direct drive actuators at rated torque, ignoring the weight of its own links. Stringman figure is for a 7 × 7 × 3 m room at the 28 N line tension limit, net of its 638 g gripper and marker.
Stringman is open source and OSHWA certified. The mechanical CAD, the PCBs, and the control software are all published.
We believe owners should be in control of their own robots. That's why Stringman can run air gapped on your local Wi-Fi network: the UI is served locally, AI models run on your own hardware, and no data ever leaves your network.
Give your home lab the capability of carrying parts from one workcell to another anywhere in the room, so you can get more out of your other robots. The Python API and MCP server is made for agents so you can get your workflow running right away.
2022 Porsche 911 GT3 RSR model by No Limits, CC BY 4.0, simplified. SO-101 arm from TheRobotStudio/SO-ARM100, Apache 2.0.
Unlike desktop arms limited to a fixed radius, Stringman leverages a cable-driven architecture to access the full volume of a room. The work area volume per dollar of this type of robot is completely unmatched, all with fewer actuators than even the simplest mobile robots. Anchors and eylets are mounted in the corners of the room near the ceiling and define a four-sided work area within which any object can be moved from point to point.
That's roughly 500× the work area volume per dollar, at comparable 2 kg payload.
Step-by-step: picture guide or video guide
The original prototype was built in a room with a ceiling fan, and it still runs there today. Mount the anchors at or below the level of the blades and the lines can't physically reach it.
Several methods are available for control with default models for automatic grasping, target, and destination selection to make it easy to quickly build new behaviors.
Stringman is fully capable of LeRobot control using including Pi.05, JEPA, Multitask DiT, and others.
Collecting training data for new behaviors can be done from the UI, and as few as 50 episodes can be enough for certain models like DiT to learn a behavior.
As long as it remains installed, yes. However, when parked, they are up near the ceiling and out of the way. Clutter on the ceiling is preferable to clutter on the floor in our opinion. If you need to remove the anchors, they can be detached from their mounts without tools, leaving a relatively small white cleat on the wall.
Yes, it's just a matter of mounting the anchors at or below the level of the fan, making it physically impossible for the lines or marker tag to touch it. Similarly, the work area can be shrunk to exclude low hanging light fixtures if they are off to the side, but if the center of the room does contain low hanging objects, Stringman cannot be installed in that room.
When reaching a tension limit of 28 newtons (about the weight of a backpack), all motors relax and the lines can be pulled loose. Since they are overhead most of the time, it's uncommon for people to collide with them.
Not by default, but if you bind it with neufangled.com/playroom then you or anyone you share access with can operate it from anywhere, and access can be revoked at any time. Neufangled Robotics does not store any of the information from your robot that is forwarded through its servers.
For those who prefer to make the trade-off by binding their robot to an account, our web-based console allows you to monitor and control Stringman from anywhere. Think of it as a security camera with a hand.
If you do decide that you would like to make use of our cloud telemetry relay, You can use it, and still go back to a completely lan only mode whenever you want. Your data is never collected.
Organizing your home is a physical process, not a coding task. Use our clip-on fiducial tags to designate your laundry bin, toy box, and trash can. Stringman maps these locations visually. You don't need to tag individual pieces of clutter—just the destination. If there's something you never want it to pick up, you can mark that item as off-limits.
Networks trained to control stringman have learned that the word "toybox" refers to that tag, so you can use it to mark anything even if it doesn't look like the toyboxes from our training set.
You can also use the tags as arbitrary source and destination markers for ferry jobs, such as carrying items from one robot arm to another. or carrying laundry from the ground to a robotic folding station
A classroom with a Stringman robot gives your students a chance to become familiar with robotics fundamentals such as inverse kinematics, telemetry, and imitation learning while controlling an exotic and capable flying gripper. If you have walls and a MacBook, you're more than halfway there.
Cross embodiment is one of the biggest challenges in robotics, and showing that a model can operate a vastly different body type is a stronger result than moving it from one bimanual robot to another. Our datasets are public on Hugging Face, there's a controller-in-the-loop MuJoCo sim, and Stringman works with LeRobot, making it one of the most inexpensive robots to test on and a natural capstone project.
Mobile robots spend a significant portion of their time charging. Because Stringman is a powered from the wall, it's always ready for work. Furthermore, by removing the heavy battery pack, we've increased the payload capacity per dollar compared to mobile platforms that must waste energy carrying their own power supply.
The gripper's power is delivered via one of the support cables. A two-conductor FEP jacketed twisted pair cable with a tensile strength of 50N.
What's that pole for? Stringman's gripper hangs below the pivot point so it can reach the floor next to beds and tables. This additional linkage could allow unconstrained motion so Stringman employs active swing cancellation algorithms to counteract momentum, without adding the cost of any additional motors. This ensures the gripper remains steady and predictable even during rapid cross-room traversals.
There's a whole video about swing cancellation if you're curious about how it works!
Often, a simple solution that gets the job done has more value than a complex one. Stringman uses a two fingered gripper with a wrist. This is enough dexterity for the clutter it is designed to pick up, keeping weight and cost low and reliability high. In our household tests we have determined that more layers of grip tape is simply a better return on investment than more articulated fingers.
The gripper can rotate it's wrist to better place the fingers around flat sided or long objects.
For a easy preview of how it looks in your room, print the anchor mockup in white PLA and hold it up in a corner. Get the files.
TThe Stringman faceplate is easily swappable. Grab the STL or bambu 3MF files to print your faceplate in any color.

Latest wave: 2 November 2026
Based on incident dates in news reports ↗
Are the fridges ok?
Supermarket refrigeration systems are still being hacked. Internet-exposed Danfoss controllers are part of the problem.
How we got here
Our baseline counts each IP once, even when it exposes several StoreView services. Shodan-tagged honeypot records are excluded, but an IP with both tagged and untagged records can remain. IP addresses are a proxy for systems, not a count of physical fridges.
Indexed StoreView IPs · tagged service records excluded
Loading measurement…
Loading total including tagged honeypots…
One IP.
Many fridges.
One public IP can front several controllers, and each controller can manage many fridges. Exposure alone does not prove compromise.
What we're measuring ↗
Still out in the open.
Historical service totals before IP deduplication and honeypot filtering. These use a different unit from the distinct-IP baseline above; they do not count compromised fridges.
These totals include tagged honeypots. Historical sources did not provide a honeypot breakdown. Published observations may use different search details and collection times. Gaps are unmeasured; points are not interpolated.
View observations & sources
Is the exposed fleet getting newer?
Daily inferred firmware mix across indexed Danfoss StoreView services worldwide. This chart is weighted by services, so one IP can contribute multiple ports; the headline baseline counts distinct IPs. These daily versions come from cached headers.
A rising share of newer versions can reflect upgrades, older systems going offline, new arrivals, or changes in Shodan's index. This chart does not follow individual devices or prove upgrades. Multiple ports can still inflate counts, and untagged honeypots may remain.
Latest version breakdown & methodology
Exact cached Last-Modified fingerprints are matched to the firmware-build timestamps published by Censys. Shared fingerprints remain ambiguous; unmatched banners remain unknown. The chart uses the same StoreView query as the headline count, with an optional honeypot exclusion. Newer StoreView Web titles were present in this query during our baseline census; this is still not a complete inventory of all Danfoss products.
Counts are collected from Shodan's existing index, not from a live vulnerability test. The queries run sequentially and are not a single atomic snapshot. The headline uses a separate distinct-IP snapshot; this chart counts services. Exposure and firmware totals may differ because Shodan answers those API requests separately. The collector rejects changing population totals or inconsistent sums and preserves the last valid observation. “4.3.1 or 5.x” is a version grouping, not an assurance that equipment is secure. Download full measurement history ↗
A pattern, not a one-off.
From suspected attacks at military bases to repeated disruption in European supermarkets.
The problem predates 2026. Danfoss also documented attacks on supermarket refrigeration in Russia and Israel in 2022. Danfoss newsletter, page 9 ↗
Cold facts.
Clear limitations.
A quiet news cycle is not an all-clear.
What does “No” mean?
This is an editorial assessment of the reported attacks and continuing exposure, not a live test of every fridge. It does not automatically turn to “Yes” after a quiet stretch.
What resets the counter?
A reviewed, substantial attack wave that disrupts refrigeration at multiple sites. We use the incident date, not the date of a later article. Suspected incidents are labeled; a new headline about an old incident does not reset the clock. Days use UTC calendar dates.
What does the Shodan number measure?
The prominent baseline counts distinct IP addresses with at least one matching service not tagged by Shodan as a honeypot; the small-print totals include tagged service records. An IP with both tagged and untagged records remains eligible. The exposure history retains unfiltered historical totals, while the firmware chart excludes tagged honeypots by default. All counts are matching internet service banners, worldwide, for http.title:"Danfoss StoreView". It is a narrow fingerprint, not all Danfoss products. Multiple ports can inflate the total; one controller can serve many fridges. Shodan's index also lags real-world changes. Download distinct-IP history ↗ · API methodology ↗
What did the one-off landing-page measurement find?
On 3 November 2026, a separately authorized active measurement made one ordinary unauthenticated request to / at one cached endpoint for each of 2,050 eligible IPs. It recognized 212 StoreView landing pages; 1,409 requests timed out and 332 had TLS failures. The remaining 97 produced other pages, responses or errors. Another 51 IPs had no eligible cached endpoint. There were no retries, redirect following, logins, scripts or controller changes.
This is a conservative observation, not a complete live-device count: timeouts and TLS failures do not establish that equipment is offline. Among recognized pages, 205 retained the cached firmware inference and seven differed or became unknown; this does not establish seven upgrades. Visible UI versions are not controller firmware. A later code audit reproduced an undercount risk: the original reader could receive a valid title, then time out waiting for more body data. The number of affected timeouts cannot be recovered, so 212 is only the number recognized by that checker. The checker has since been corrected and tested locally; this measurement has not been rerun.
A later cached Shodan query found 106 IPs with honeypot-tagged StoreView records. The original filter excluded tagged records, rather than every IP with any tagged record. The overlap between those IPs and the 212 recognized pages is unknown because no IP-to-outcome linkage was retained. Download the cached honeypot audit ↗. Only aggregate results are retained. Daily updates continue to use cached Shodan data; this active measurement is not scheduled. Download the aggregate report ↗
How does this stay up to date?
GitHub Actions requests aggregate Shodan IP, service and firmware counts daily at 11:17 UTC and saves their dated history. News is reviewed separately each day by a scheduled Codex task; its last completed review is shown above. Failed collections preserve prior data and show its age. Historical published snapshots remain separate from our own samples.
How can operators reduce exposure?
Follow the manufacturer's and your national CERT's guidance: restrict access to management interfaces, use protected remote access, and apply supported updates. Internet exposure does not by itself identify an exploited vulnerability. Read CERT-FR's advisory ↗
