articles.title: Bear turns 10, and it still feels like day one
articles.body:
Back in 2013, three friends who loved Apple and design couldn’t find a notes app they liked, so they built their own. That side project became Bear. It arrived on the App Store in November 2016, and within a year it had been named Mac App of the Year and won an Apple Design Award. This November, the little Bear turns 10. Today it helps millions of people around the world capture their ideas and organize their lives every day, and we’ve felt so much love and support from all of you along the way.
The idea
We couldn’t find a notes app that fit how we write, so we started building our own.
More
We built it in our spare time. Our day job back then was building apps and websites for clients.
First prototype
Our friends loved it. Would everyone else?
Launch day!
Bear arrives on the App Store and hits #1 on Product Hunt.
Mac App of the Year
Apple names Bear its Mac App of the Year.
Apple Design Award
Bear wins a 2017 Apple Design Award.
More
…and we got a selfie with Tim Cook!
Project Panda
We start rewriting Bear’s editor from scratch, code name “Panda”.
More
Your feedback showed us where the original Bear was hitting its limits. Six months in, we realized we needed our own Markdown parser too, so we started over. Again.
Bear 2 is here!
Bear 2 launches with an all-new editor and 20+ new features.
Bear Web beta
Bear comes to your browser in public beta.
Bear Web
The full release of Bear Web is almost here, and we have more features brewing in house…
Over the years, one thing we hear again and again is that Bear just feels good to use. So for this special occasion, we want to share the principles behind every design decision we make. Along the way you’ll find some tiny details we’ve hidden all over the app (you may be using a few right now without knowing it), a peek at an idea that never shipped, and some brand new Bear swag. Grab a slice of cake and come on in!
Bear Principles
Every change in Bear goes through a long journey from first idea to final release. Big or small, visible or under the hood, they all follow the same two principles: Bear should be delightful to use, and safe to trust.
A feeling-good experience by design
We want you to feel delighted every time you open Bear. In practice, that comes down to three things.
Simple. No sign up, no tutorial. Just open a note and write. Bear has grown much more powerful over the years, but all of that power waits quietly underneath and never gets in your way.
💡 Did you know?
To make sure Bear stays easy to use, we always ask our parents to test it first!
Natural. We believe the best tools disappear while you use them. So we put a lot of effort into making things work exactly the way you expect, and you’ll find these quality of life touches all over the app.
Take moving lines around. Press ⌘⌥ with the up or down arrow to move the current line, which is perfect for rearranging your writing. Bear understands what you’re moving and where it’s going, so it won’t break apart a list or a table along the way. It’s one of those things that feels so obvious you’d never guess someone had to design it.
Rewarding to explore. Bear has a lot of depth, but we don’t believe in pushing everything to your face to promote it because we don’t know when or if you will need them. Many of our favorite user stories start with a happy little accident. Resize an image from its corner, and it snaps to line up with the images around it; swipe left on a note on iOS, and the Info Panel slides into view. We love those “Oh wow, I didn’t expect that to work!” moments. They’re a big part of why we sign off every post with “Happy writing!”
💡 Did you know?
Some of our favorite details are so small that you may be using them without ever noticing. Here are a few to try:
✍️ Typing in bold or italic? Press Return or the same shortcut again to step right out of the style.
⌨️ Press ⌘A inside a code block to select just the code. Press it again to select the whole note.
🖱️ Select some text and type (, [, " or`. Bear wraps your selection instead of replacing it.
🔗 Select some text and paste a URL. The text becomes a link.
Built to be safe
You can’t feel truly comfortable in a space you don’t trust. Your notes hold your ideas, your plans, and sometimes things you’d never share with anyone. That’s why safety has shaped Bear’s most fundamental choices from the very start.
Private. We have no servers holding your notes, and we never see what you write. We also don’t build Bear on top of third party APIs, plugins, or outside services we can’t control. If one of them changed its rules, shut down, or simply stopped working, you would be the one paying the price. So we build what matters ourselves, and Bear keeps working the way you expect.
💡 Did you know?
We collaborated with Cossack Labs for note encryption to ensure a reliable and smooth experience. Even if your iCloud account were ever hacked, you can rest assured your encrypted notes stay unreadable.
Keeping a note taking app private and standard wasn’t a revolutionary idea in 2016 when we first launched Bear, but today, it kind of is. And we are glad we stick to what we believe since day 1. The world is changing and we don’t know where it leads us to, but we know your notes are safe with us and you have full control of them anytime, anywhere.
How features get made
Every design in Bear starts with a problem: a feature people need, something that’s broken, or simply something we don’t like. From there, we are on a journey of problem solving.
That usually means a designer and a developer pairing up for a week or two, then bringing something working to the whole team. Then the real fun begins. Matteo, one of our cofounders, describes fun as “clashing heads with wonderful people to make great things.” Everyone in the team gets to express their opinions no matter what title they have. As a matter of fact, job titles mean nothing to us as you can see on our website.
The feedback discussion can be brutal. “No” is a very welcome answer here, with one house rule: you have to give a reason. Wall of text and hour long slack huddles come and go, then the paring up buddies return to the improvement part and provide a second round, a third round, until we are all happy with it. There are lucky days that some ideas get a big yes on the first try. Others spark weeks and months of debate and never ship at all. We’d rather be a little stubborn about what feels like Bear than chase every trend.
💡 Did you know?
Back in 2022, we had the idea to create a fourth column for the info panel, TOC, and Backlinks in Bear 2 update. The concept was discussed internally and also shared with on our forum, but at the end we were not convinced by the design at practical level, and thus the feature was never born in Bear 2.
A milestone, and more to come
Over the years, Bear has grown up much bigger than we expected with millions of users enjoying Bear everyday. We’ve seen so many different ways of using Bear: prepare teaching materials in school, work as their second brain, or just write grocery lists (yes, that’s our parents!). 10 years is a huge milestone for us and we want to say a huge thank you to everyone no matter if you have been here since day 1 with us, or just downloaded Bear two minutes ago.
We won’t hand you a flashy roadmap, but here’s what we can say for sure. Bear Web is almost ready for its full release, and we’re also working on note versioning and some other top secret things. Beyond that, we’ll keep doing what we’ve done for ten years: working our best to provide you a comfortable, private space to create beautiful notes.
🎁 Present time!
Kumagotchi: a writing pal for your Home Screen
Meet Kumagotchi1, a cute pixel bear who lives in a widget on your Home Screen and keeps you company while you write. Its status quietly follows how you use Bear: it strolls around the meadow when you’ve opened Bear recently, scribbles in its own little notebook while you write, watches the clouds while you read, and takes a nap in the grass when you’ve been away for a while. It’s as old as your very first note, and its weight grows with every note you write.
Six new app icons
What’s a birthday without a little dress up? We’ve crafted six new app icons2 for the occasion: a special 10th anniversary icon, Bear with Birdie, a golden Bear, a peeking Bear, and two classic pixel Bears. We hope they bring a bit of fun to your Home Screen, and a gentle reminder to enjoy the little things in life.
Did somebody say Bear swag?
Yes, they are finally here! Many of you have been asking for Bear merch and we have been secretly working on them! Our 10th anniversary merch features pixel art of a classic Macintosh with the Bear logo glowing on its screen and our little Birdie perched on top, a nod to where it all began. Check our merch page below to grab your Bear swag!
See you in the next decade
Thank you for being part of the story, whether you’ve been here since day one or found Bear last week. We’d love to hear about your favorite hidden detail, or one you just discovered in this post. Come say happy birthday to us on our Community Forum, Reddit, X (Twitter), Bluesky, or directly at bear@shinyfrog.net.
Happy Writing!
🐻❤️📝

Today it helps millions of people around the world capture their ideas and organize their lives every day, and we’ve felt so much love and support from all of you along the way.
The idea
We couldn’t find a notes app that fit how we write, so we started building our own.
More
We built it in our spare time. Our day job back then was building apps and websites for clients.
First prototype
Our friends loved it. Would everyone else?
Launch day!
Bear arrives on the App Store and hits #1 on Product Hunt.
Mac App of the Year
Apple names Bear its Mac App of the Year.
Apple Design Award
Bear wins a 2017 Apple Design Award.
More
…and we got a selfie with Tim Cook!
Project Panda
We start rewriting Bear’s editor from scratch, code name “Panda”.
More
Your feedback showed us where the original Bear was hitting its limits. Six months in, we realized we needed our own Markdown parser too, so we started over. Again.
Bear 2 is here!
Bear 2 launches with an all-new editor and 20+ new features.
Bear Web beta
Bear comes to your browser in public beta.
Bear Web
The full release of Bear Web is almost here, and we have more features brewing in house…
Over the years, one thing we hear again and again is that Bear just feels good to use. So for this special occasion, we want to share the principles behind every design decision we make. Along the way you’ll find some tiny details we’ve hidden all over the app (you may be using a few right now without knowing it), a peek at an idea that never shipped, and some brand new Bear swag. Grab a slice of cake and come on in!
Bear Principles
Every change in Bear goes through a long journey from first idea to final release. Big or small, visible or under the hood, they all follow the same two principles: Bear should be delightful to use, and safe to trust.
A feeling-good experience by design
We want you to feel delighted every time you open Bear. In practice, that comes down to three things.
Simple. No sign up, no tutorial. Just open a note and write. Bear has grown much more powerful over the years, but all of that power waits quietly underneath and never gets in your way.
💡 Did you know?
To make sure Bear stays easy to use, we always ask our parents to test it first!
Natural. We believe the best tools disappear while you use them. So we put a lot of effort into making things work exactly the way you expect, and you’ll find these quality of life touches all over the app.
Take moving lines around. Press ⌘⌥ with the up or down arrow to move the current line, which is perfect for rearranging your writing. Bear understands what you’re moving and where it’s going, so it won’t break apart a list or a table along the way. It’s one of those things that feels so obvious you’d never guess someone had to design it.
Rewarding to explore. Bear has a lot of depth, but we don’t believe in pushing everything to your face to promote it because we don’t know when or if you will need them. Many of our favorite user stories start with a happy little accident. Resize an image from its corner, and it snaps to line up with the images around it; swipe left on a note on iOS, and the Info Panel slides into view. We love those “Oh wow, I didn’t expect that to work!” moments. They’re a big part of why we sign off every post with “Happy writing!”
💡 Did you know?
Some of our favorite details are so small that you may be using them without ever noticing. Here are a few to try:
✍️ Typing in bold or italic? Press Return or the same shortcut again to step right out of the style.
⌨️ Press ⌘A inside a code block to select just the code. Press it again to select the whole note.
🖱️ Select some text and type (, [, " or`. Bear wraps your selection instead of replacing it.
🔗 Select some text and paste a URL. The text becomes a link.
Built to be safe
You can’t feel truly comfortable in a space you don’t trust. Your notes hold your ideas, your plans, and sometimes things you’d never share with anyone. That’s why safety has shaped Bear’s most fundamental choices from the very start.
Private. We have no servers holding your notes, and we never see what you write. We also don’t build Bear on top of third party APIs, plugins, or outside services we can’t control. If one of them changed its rules, shut down, or simply stopped working, you would be the one paying the price. So we build what matters ourselves, and Bear keeps working the way you expect.
💡 Did you know?
We collaborated with Cossack Labs for note encryption to ensure a reliable and smooth experience. Even if your iCloud account were ever hacked, you can rest assured your encrypted notes stay unreadable.
Keeping a note taking app private and standard wasn’t a revolutionary idea in 2016 when we first launched Bear, but today, it kind of is. And we are glad we stick to what we believe since day 1. The world is changing and we don’t know where it leads us to, but we know your notes are safe with us and you have full control of them anytime, anywhere.
How features get made
Every design in Bear starts with a problem: a feature people need, something that’s broken, or simply something we don’t like. From there, we are on a journey of problem solving.
That usually means a designer and a developer pairing up for a week or two, then bringing something working to the whole team. Then the real fun begins. Matteo, one of our cofounders, describes fun as “clashing heads with wonderful people to make great things.” Everyone in the team gets to express their opinions no matter what title they have. As a matter of fact, job titles mean nothing to us as you can see on our website.
The feedback discussion can be brutal. “No” is a very welcome answer here, with one house rule: you have to give a reason. Wall of text and hour long slack huddles come and go, then the paring up buddies return to the improvement part and provide a second round, a third round, until we are all happy with it. There are lucky days that some ideas get a big yes on the first try. Others spark weeks and months of debate and never ship at all. We’d rather be a little stubborn about what feels like Bear than chase every trend.
💡 Did you know?
Back in 2022, we had the idea to create a fourth column for the info panel, TOC, and Backlinks in Bear 2 update. The concept was discussed internally and also shared with on our forum, but at the end we were not convinced by the design at practical level, and thus the feature was never born in Bear 2.
A milestone, and more to come
Over the years, Bear has grown up much bigger than we expected with millions of users enjoying Bear everyday. We’ve seen so many different ways of using Bear: prepare teaching materials in school, work as their second brain, or just write grocery lists (yes, that’s our parents!). 10 years is a huge milestone for us and we want to say a huge thank you to everyone no matter if you have been here since day 1 with us, or just downloaded Bear two minutes ago.
We won’t hand you a flashy roadmap, but here’s what we can say for sure. Bear Web is almost ready for its full release, and we’re also working on note versioning and some other top secret things. Beyond that, we’ll keep doing what we’ve done for ten years: working our best to provide you a comfortable, private space to create beautiful notes.
🎁 Present time!
Kumagotchi: a writing pal for your Home Screen
Meet Kumagotchi1, a cute pixel bear who lives in a widget on your Home Screen and keeps you company while you write. Its status quietly follows how you use Bear: it strolls around the meadow when you’ve opened Bear recently, scribbles in its own little notebook while you write, watches the clouds while you read, and takes a nap in the grass when you’ve been away for a while. It’s as old as your very first note, and its weight grows with every note you write.
Six new app icons
What’s a birthday without a little dress up? We’ve crafted six new app icons2 for the occasion: a special 10th anniversary icon, Bear with Birdie, a golden Bear, a peeking Bear, and two classic pixel Bears. We hope they bring a bit of fun to your Home Screen, and a gentle reminder to enjoy the little things in life.
Did somebody say Bear swag?
Yes, they are finally here! Many of you have been asking for Bear merch and we have been secretly working on them! Our 10th anniversary merch features pixel art of a classic Macintosh with the Bear logo glowing on its screen and our little Birdie perched on top, a nod to where it all began. Check our merch page below to grab your Bear swag!
See you in the next decade
Thank you for being part of the story, whether you’ve been here since day one or found Bear last week. We’d love to hear about your favorite hidden detail, or one you just discovered in this post. Come say happy birthday to us on our Community Forum, Reddit, X (Twitter), Bluesky, or directly at bear@shinyfrog.net.
Happy Writing!
🐻❤️📝

articles.title: Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?
articles.body:
by Nicholas Carlini 2026-11-01
On February 10th, 1996, a computer program (IBM's Deep Blue) defeated the reigning chess champion (Garry Kasparov) in a game of chess for the first time. Deep Blue would go on to lose the match, but a year later, would get its revenge in a 3.5-2.5 rematch.
In order to achieve this feat, IBM spent several million dollars on research and development building a special-purpose computer specifically for this purpose. Deep Blue itself (the victorious, upgraded version) was powered by 30 P2SC processors each running at roughly 120 MHz, and (most importantly) 480 custom VLSI chess co-processors used to perform chess-specific operations like move generation and position evaluation. When it was built, Deep Blue was the 259th most powerful supercomputer in the world, and could analyze over 200 million chess positions per second.
But was Deep Blue necessary to beat Kasparov? Or could we have gotten away with an off-the-shelf 1996 desktop running a smarter chess engine?
As it turns out, we could easily have beaten Kasparov without building Deep Blue, using only commodity hardware, and it (almost certainly) wouldn't have even been close. I know this because, as I write this very sentence, I have sitting next to me a 200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro (released exactly 31 years ago---November 1st, 1995) with 64MB of RAM running a custom port of Stockfish that plays at an estimated Elo of 3300 ± 87 at classical time controls---far beyond the strength of any human, or indeed Kasparov's Elo of just under 2800. But wait, there's more! I've hooked this machine up to the internet with a Realtek RTL8139C Ethernet card, so you can play it below!
There are three ways to get stronger at chess: you can analyze more moves, analyze better moves, or analyze moves better. Famously, humans improve by doing the latter two: the average chess grandmaster during a classical game will analyze roughly the same number of moves as an amateur player, but they analyze only the most critical moves and do a better job with that analysis. Chess engines like Stockfish, running on silicon instead of our human brains, dominate us at the first of these and analyze millions of positions per second. And because there's not that much room for micro-optimizations on modern engines that will let a given CPU process more positions per second, most progress in chess AI also tends to follow how humans improve and finds better methods for selecting moves and analyzing boards.
Skill in chess is measured by an Elo score. A difference of 200 Elo means that you should expect the stronger player to win three out of every four games, and multiplicatively from there: a 400 Elo gap corresponds to a 90% expected score and a 1000 Elo gap gives a 99.7% expected score. The best chess engines that you could run on commodity 1996 hardware were rated roughly 2300 Elo. Deep Blue was rated 2700. In contrast, modern Stockfish is rated closer to 3700.
This raises the question: how much of the advantage of a modern chess engine comes down to the fact that a modern desktop computer is extremely fast, and how much of the advantage comes down to the fact that we've just gotten better at programming chess engines? As it turns out, the majority of the Elo gains (+720 of the +1335 gained) can be attributed to better programming, and not better hardware.
To test this, I ran two experiments. The first experiment uses Crafty, a competitive engine from 1996 whose source code is now available. On my Pentium Pro, the 1996 build of Crafty version 11.13 has an Elo of 1999 ± 90 at 1 second per move, and 2383 ± 77 at 10 seconds per move. On modern hardware (a Ryzen 7) this engine's Elo jumps massively to 2614 ± 97 at the same 1 second per move. But if I take this engine and slowly start to add all the knowledge we have about how to design better chess engines---adding modern search algorithms like fail-soft, LMR, correction history; adding better quiescence methods; and adding neural-net evals (NNUE)---then you can increase the Elo up to 2718 ± 34 on the Pentium Pro at 1 second per move, and 2974 ± 74 at 10 seconds per move.
In the second experiment I go somewhat further: instead of trying to update Crafty, let's just try to get Stockfish---the best chess engine today---running on 1996 hardware and see how it does. This takes some work and is mainly a matter of rewriting the code so that it uses 32-bit arithmetic (a PPro is a 32-bit machine) and doesn't use more than 64MB of RAM. This naive port has an Elo of roughly 2496 ± 64 at 1 second per move (2940 ± 76 at 10 seconds per move). But we can do better! A modern Stockfish engine is designed to run on a modern CPU. By making a number of adjustments to the algorithm and tuning it to the Pentium, we can increase its Elo to 2846 ± 35 at 1 second per move, 3109 ± 79 at 10 seconds per move, and 3180 ± 80 at 30 seconds per move.
The most concise way to summarize all of the above is just to have them play a match of 100 games against each other. And when I do this, I find that a modern chess engine running on a 1996 Pentium Pro wins 78, draws 17, and loses 5 games against the 1996 Crafty engine running on modern hardware.
The remainder of this article provides the details.
There's not much to say about the hardware, to be honest. I bought a used ("vintage" said the listing; I feel old.) desktop PC with standard period-appropriate hardware. The desktop is running a 200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro connected to an Intel VS440FX motherboard with 64MB of SIMM RAM clocked at 66 MHz. The operating system boot off of a 1.44MB 3.5 inch floppy disk, and connect to the Internet via a Realtek RTL8139C. I also have a 1MB Trio64V+ graphics card connected over VGA to my monitor, with input coming from a PS/2 keyboard---but I don't much use either of those and instead communicate with it over a serial port connected to my modern desktop.
For those readers who may not be able to appropriately contextualize this hardware, a 200 MHz Pentium Pro sold for $1,325 at launch in November 1995, and four 16 MB SIMMs would have cost about $2,000. Add on the other peripherals, and this machine would likely have gone for about four or five thousand dollars. So it's a nice workstation, but by no means a supercomputer. However, given the rate of depreciation and the exponential rate of improvements to hardware, this same machine in 1997, when the second match occurred, would likely go for just a thousand dollars (because who would want to buy a Pentium Pro when the better-in-almost-every-way Pentium MMX was now available for just $400?)
The interface between the chess engine and the internet is a custom-built "operating system" whose sole job is to spin up the chess engine and connect it directly to the networking card. (Throughout this article, when I say "I wrote", what I really mean is "I asked an LLM to write". I used a combination of Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 to implement the code here. (This article, though, is human text.).) It's designed to be as compact as possible: the operating system (which, in fact, is more like a hypervisor, or something) is sitting on a bootable floppy disk. Its sole job is to boot the Pentium Pro into 32-bit protected mode, initialize the networking card, and await further instructions. I can then send it any arbitrary "userspace" guest program that I want into RAM and it'll boot that up and start running it. The chess program I wrote starts up a custom-built HTTP server which waits for incoming HTTP requests with a given position (as a FEN string) and maximum run time, and on each request runs the engine until the timer expires, and returns a response.
As mentioned earlier I (again: a language model) actually modified two engines. The stronger of the two is powered by Stockfish adapted to run efficiently on a thirty-year-old processor. It plays at an estimated Elo of 3300 at classical time controls Because I can't run nearly enough games at classical time controls on my single machine to get this number, I've extrapolated it from shorter time controls. I measured 3180 ± 80 at 30 seconds per move, and it gained +70 Elo per tripling of the time between 1 second to 10 seconds and 10 seconds to 30 seconds. Because a classical game gives about six minutes per move (including thinking on the opponent's turn) we should expect an Elo of 3350. Allowing for some diminishing returns, a safe estimate is an Elo of 3300. , high enough above Kasparov's 2800 Elo that we should expect Stockfish-1996 to come out ahead with a score of roughly 9/10. The (only slightly) weaker engine starts with the source code to Crafty 11.13, and is brought forward in time by adding all the lessons we've learned about how to write a better chess engine over the past thirty years.
The first engine I (read: my LLM) worked on was Crafty 11.13, its 1996 release. On this engine the LLM had to do the most work to backport ideas we've learned over the last 30 years. Below is a breakdown of where the Elo gains come from, when evaluating either at 1 second per move or 10 seconds per move. Sometimes you'll find the 1s vs 10s improvements disagree. Part of this clearly could be noise---I only ran a few hundred games which leaves a relatively large margin of error---but there is also quite a lot of signal here. Because the 1996 computer is so much slower, at 1s/move it has a very low search depth and so how fast the evaluation runs matters more than how good it is. But at larger search depths, once you stop making tactical blunders, the position evaluation becomes much more important.
On the second engine, as mentioned above, I did the inverse. I (again, read: my LLM) ported Stockfish to run on 1996 hardware, and then tweaked the parameters so that it would be better suited to lower search depth. The gains here are thus somewhat more modest, because there are no large algorithm wins that remain.
I think it's overwhelmingly likely to be the case, but it's actually a little bit more tricky of a situation than you might hope. You see, I've done a bit of sleight of hand throughout this article. The problem is that Elo scores are relative, and I've been comparing my engine's Elo to that of various Stockfish engines that have known strengths on the Computer Chess Rating Lists (CCRL). But because humans don't play against engines very frequently, there can be some small divergences between scores on the FIDE Elo ladder and the CCRL ladder, in the same way a player's FIDE Elo doesn't directly translate to their Elo on online chess. Fortunately, because I've gotten these engines to play at an Elo rating of 3200-3300, and Kasparov was rated just under 2800, there should be more than sufficient buffer to absorb any discrepancy.
But if you happen to know a 2700+ Super GM who wants to try and defeat a 2026 chess engine playing on 1996 hardware, I'd be happy to accept the challenge!
The first time we humans do anything, we rarely do it efficiently. Once we see a path that would clearly work if only we scaled it up, we do just that. Only later, after we've had the time to better understand the problem at hand, do we come to recognize that we could have achieved the same feat much more efficiently by being clever.
I mostly did this for fun, because whether I could have beaten Kasparov with commodity hardware sounded like a fun question to answer, but I also hoped it would provide a tiny bit of insight into the rate of algorithmic progress in "AI". Chess engines in 1997 were already quite advanced; after all, Alan Turing helped write the first chess program nearly fifty years earlier. So I suppose at the time it seemed plausible that maybe there weren't that many more ideas left to find. And with hindsight it's easy to see that's wrong.
Which leads to the question: just how much are we leaving on the table with modern-day "AI"---that is to say, language models. Will the advances we accrue over the next few years from software outpace the advances in hardware scale? Clearly this toy experiment doesn't answer that question definitively, but it does gesture at a potential future. (There's also probably some kind of meta-lesson about using LLMs---"AI"---to speed up our ability to answer weird research questions like this.)
(Also, uh, if anyone has any ideas for projects I could do with a Pentium Pro in a few weeks once I no longer need it to host this chess engine ... do let me know!)

Which leads to the question: just how much are we leaving on the table with modern-day "AI"---that is to say, language models. Will the advances we accrue over the next few years from software outpace the advances in hardware scale? Clearly this toy experiment doesn't answer that question definitively, but it does gesture at a potential future. (There's also probably some kind of meta-lesson about using LLMs---"AI"---to speed up our ability to answer weird research questions like this.)
(Also, uh, if anyone has any ideas for projects I could do with a Pentium Pro in a few weeks once I no longer need it to host this chess engine ... do let me know!)

articles.title: Binance Says Hackers Used Fake Job Interviews, AI Tool to Steal $6.3 Billion In Crypto
articles.body:
Binance Says Hackers Used Fake Job Interviews, AI Tool to Steal $6.3 Billion In Crypto 8
			
		 	
				Binance says hackers spent months infiltrating its systems through fake job interviews, a tampered developer tool and compromised internal AI tools before stealing $6.34 billion in crypto in the Oct. 29 attack. Co-CEO Richard Teng said Binance has replenished 98% of the affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets. CNBC reports:  Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker."
[...] As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street."
"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

articles.title: WorkOS reports security breach
articles.body:
It's not on their website or Trust center yet, but we received the following breach notification from WorkOS:
We are writing to notify you of a data security incident that we detected on October 30, 2026 and are continuing to investigate. We value your trust and want to keep you informed while our investigation continues.
What Happened
On October 30, 2026, at 16:39 UTC, WorkOS detected anomalous traffic to an internal business system. Our investigation identified evidence the attack was likely driven by ARTEX, an AI-assisted, autonomous penetration testing framework, from IP addresses based in Hong Kong and China.
The unauthorized actor gained access to an internal API used by our sales and marketing tools. Through this service, it was able to access data from our Salesforce and Snowflake instances. These systems hold business contact information, account and commercial information, aggregated and de-identified product usage metrics, marketing contacts, and support tickets. This includes CRM information such as names, email addresses, phone numbers, company mailing addresses, and other business information for WorkOS customers.
We have no evidence that your application data was accessed. We also have no evidence that any production WorkOS services were accessed or impacted. Our current analysis indicates this incident was localized to only CRM and customer support data.

articles.title: Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
articles.body:
Starting today, Siri can tune into the Apple Watch’s mic with Audio Intelligence features that are available in the new watchOS 27.3 developer beta rolling out now. The two new additions are Siri Recap, which uses “ambient listening” to generate summaries of your conversation, and Live Rewind, which generates text transcripts of the last 15 seconds of audio your watch’s mic detected.
Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
Audio Intelligence lets Siri ‘rewind’ and summarize audio from your Watch’s mic.
Apple is also releasing its redesigned Health app for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. It adds sections like a new Insights tab with summaries for heart, sleep, fitness, and other data that pop up during the day, a For You section with personalized recommendations, and health content like educational videos and articles.
- Live Rewind, which can help users recall what was just said in conversation. A double-press of the Digital Crown shows the previous 15 seconds of a conversation as a text snippet, so the user can catch something they may have missed or are less familiar with. Users can ask Siri about the content of the text or save it to the Siri app to revisit later.
- Siri Recap, which can create high-level summaries of conversations that users can review later to jog their memory. When Siri Recap is turned on, after a conversation, Apple Intelligence automatically generates a title and key points in the new Siri app, allowing users to be more present and engaged in the moment.
When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released this Audio Intelligence
Privacy Overview (pdf) about how it plans to protect users’ privacy when their watch is listening around the clock. It goes into detail about Apple’s claims that users’ raw audio “is handled within dedicated hardware, is not saved as a file, and is not accessible to the operating system, apps, or Apple.” According to Apple, “If you use iCloud with two-factor authentication and have a device passcode, any Siri Recap summary or Live Rewind text snippet you choose to save syncs across your devices end-to-end encrypted in the Siri app.”

articles.title: Jeffrey Gibson’s ‘A Real Love Thing’ Surveys a Decade of the Artist’s Multidisciplinary Practice
articles.body:
Jeffrey Gibson’s ‘A Real Love Thing’ Surveys a Decade of the Artist’s Multidisciplinary Practice
Through abstract, prismatic acrylic paintings to garment-like sculptures and textile collages, Jeffrey Gibson explores questions of identity, lineage, and cultural translation. Working across media, the artist intricately beads monumental works and incorporates a wide range of fabrics and materials.
Jeffrey Gibson: A Real Love Thing at Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center delves into the cross-disciplinary breadth of the artist’s practice throughout the past decade. Fifteen works amplify his interest in pattern, queer iconography, and his Indigenous Mississippi Choctaw and Cherokee heritage. Drawing on the early and continuing influence of music, the artist often integrates song lyrics into tapestry-like wall hangings and three-dimensional works.
Music also inspired the title of the exhibition, which Gibson drew from a 1971 interview with soul artist Marvin Gaye, who described his seminal album What’s Going On by saying, “I think I’ve got a real love thing going. I love people, I love life, and I love nature, and I can’t see why other people can’t be like that.”
Reflecting this sentiment, Gibson’s approach is a luminous celebration of Indigenous symbolism and traditional materials, such as jingle cones used in ceremonial garments, tipi poles, and glass beads that have coated bags, moccasins, and other apparel hand-crafted by Native Americans throughout the centuries. The artist also posits a future full of hope, joy, acceptance, and, like Gaye, a love-above-all ethos.
A Real Love Thing continues through March 13 at the Bloomberg Center in Washington, D.C., where Gibson will present a talk as part of the esteemed Sam Gilliam Lecture series on November 12. And if you’re near Eugene, Oregon, the artist’s traveling solo exhibition They Teach Love is also on view through through March 7 at the University of Oregon.

articles.title: Google’s Gemini-powered Home Speaker is already on sale for 20 percent off
articles.body:
If you’re looking for a good smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker is down to around $79 ($20 off) in all four colors at Best Buy, Walmart, and Target. That’s the best price we’ve seen for the Gemini-powered speaker, which launched in June and represents Google’s first smart speaker in several years.
Google’s Gemini-powered Home Speaker is already on sale for 20 percent off
Google’s latest smart speaker offers surprisingly good sound for its size, Gemini-powered voice controls, and more.
In her review, my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy noted that Google’s new Home Speaker offers a nice balance of sound quality, size, and design. It’s smaller than the prior-gen Nest Audio, making it easy to place anywhere in your home. However, despite its small size, it produces loud, clear audio with 360-degree sound. Our own David Pierce even found it sounded cleaner, louder, and sharper than Amazon’s similarly priced Echo Dot Max, though Tuohy preferred the latter’s fuller sound and stronger bass. The older Nest Audio still sounds better overall, but Google’s latest speaker takes up less space and costs slightly less.
The Google Home Speaker also offers a few useful smart home upgrades. It supports Matter and includes a Thread border router, allowing you to connect and control a wide range of compatible smart home devices. It’s also the first Google smart speaker that can double as an audio output for the Google TV Streamer 4K, letting you play TV audio through one or two speakers instead of your TV’s built-in speakers. Tuohy found it worked well and delivered clear dialogue, though sound quality varied depending on what she was watching.
One of its most notable features is support for Gemini, which is also available on older Google speakers and is much better at understanding natural language and complex requests than the old Google Assistant. In her testing, Tuohy found it could handle multiple smart home commands at once and respond to conversational requests, like turning down the air conditioner when she mentioned feeling too hot. It’s also particularly impressive at answering general knowledge questions, though it can be slow and unreliable at times. Keep in mind, too, that some features require a $10-a-month Google Home Premium subscription, including Gemini Live, which lets you have extended conversations with the assistant without repeating the wake word.

articles.title: Tell HN: Please Vote
articles.body:
The strongest sign of a healthy democracy is that people participate in it.  It's up to you to decide who to vote for, but no matter who you support, please show up and cast a ballot.  A democracy with 75% voter turnout is healthier than a democracy with 50% voter turnout even exactly the same politicians got elected, because citizens participating in a democratic process signals that they value the process and want to keep it.
(Obviously, this only applies to people eligible to vote in ongoing elections.  If you're not eligible to vote, please don't vote.)

articles.title: You can’t hit a wrong note when playing along with songs on Casio’s new keyboard
articles.body:
Casio announced a new addition to its Casiotone line of portable electronic keyboards with a feature that could help aspiring musicians master skills like rhythm and timing without the frustrations or discouragement of hitting the wrong note.
You can’t hit a wrong note when playing along with songs on Casio’s new keyboard
The $400 CT-FS1 features Casio’s Feel Sync technology that helps inexperienced musicians hit only the right notes.
The Casiotone CT-FS1 is available now for $399.99 in a monochromatic black or white version where even the 61 touch-responsive keys are all the same color. It can run on AA batteries or a power adapter but at just under 10 pounds in weight it’s definitely not the smallest of portable keyboards. There’s built-in stereo speakers and Bluetooth connectivity if you’re playing for others, as well as a physical headphone jack.
The keyboard’s most compelling feature is what Casio calls its Feel Sync technology that works alongside a new Feel Sync mobile app available for iOS and Android devices. Through the app you can import a song file which is analyzed by an algorithm before playing through the keyboard. As you play along with the song the keyboard will only produce notes that match the song’s harmony, no matter what keys you press. You’re still responsible for timing and matching the song’s rhythm, but the keyboard takes care of everything else so you can work on developing your creative expression without being self-conscious about it sounding awful.
The CT-FS1 can be played like a standard keyboard without the Feel Sync assistance, but because it’s long enough to accommodate two musicians, you can also split the keyboard into two zones. One side works like a traditional keyboard for an experienced musician to play, while the other benefits from the real time Feel Sync corrections.

articles.title: Google Will Turn Off Search For Schools That Reject AI
articles.body:
Google Will Turn Off Search For Schools That Reject AI 32
			
		 	
				Google will disable AI tools by default for K-12 students early next year unless school administrators explicitly enable them, but schools that choose to block AI entirely will also lose student access to Google Search. The New York Times reports:  Executives at the tech giant said they wanted to be responsive to educators and parents who have asked for more control in how children interact with A.I. But there is a catch: Schools that choose to restrict A.I. entirely will also lose access to Google search. A.I. features are now a standard part of Google's commercially available search engine.
"Search and A.I. are deeply integrated," said Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google. If a school has banned A.I., he added, students "will not have access to search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available." [...] The company's new strategy underscores Google's powerful role in American education. If school leaders want continued student access to search within the company's ecosystem, they will be forced to embrace Google's A.I.

articles.title: Study Claims Vizio Simply Ignores 'Smart' TV Spying Opt Out Requests
articles.body:
Study Claims Vizio Simply Ignores 'Smart' TV Spying Opt Out Requests (techdirt.com) 59
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Techdirt: Recently, reports emerged that LG TVs are sniffing around your local network, and even listening to your local environment, even when the TV is purportedly "off." Some of those voice commands were then stored in plain text and uploaded to the internet. LG's response? To deny everything. [...] That latter point is central to a new study out of Northeastern that conducted 5,943 experiments across twelve commercial "smart" TV devices. The researchers found that most smart TVs utilize automatic content recognition (ACR), a technology that captures audio or video snapshots of viewed content and then monetizes that data to help build personalized profiles of viewers.
TV makers insist that users are supposed to be able to opt out, but the choice simply doesn't work across a large segment of TVs. Companies like Vizio simply ignored the consumer requests entirely more often than not: "We find that the advertised ACR opt-out fully suppresses ACR-attributable traffic on only four operating systems; on Samsung Tizen traffic consistent with ACR activity persists in more
than 60% of evaluated scenarios, and on Vizio SmartCast a content correlated endpoint hosted on Amazon Kinesis continues to receive traffic in 100% of opted-out scenarios."
[...] The researchers say since they can't see the precise scope of what's being collected due to encryption, they're unsure whether Vizio is technically violating its FTC agreement (not that we have a current FTC that would care if they were): "The opt-out setting has no observable effect on traffic sent to this endpoint; however, we cannot inspect the payload due to encryption so we cannot confirm whether this violates the FTC settlement." Results of whether opting out of ACR tracking actually stopped ACR tracking were all over the map. Roku, for example, ignores opt-out requests when users are watching Roku's own channels. None of the smart TV vendors track Netflix viewing for fear of violating agreements with the streaming giant. Samsung's opt out function was more likely to actually work when a user was watching antenna broadcasts.
On two Smart TV platforms, personal viewing data collected by ACR remains unencrypted, despite years of bad press and scandal on the subject. Many appear to be violating the law, but because U.S. regulatory oversight has been gutted, they see no meaningful accountability. That includes smart TV OS' like VIDAA, which is most prominently found on Hisense and Toshiba smart TVs: "VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it. Each message carries a Client ID, a permanent identifier for the TV that can't be reset, along with the time zone, the app name, the input (antenna, HDMI), the antenna channel and an audio fingerprint."

articles.title: Revolut moves to self-hosted GLM
articles.body:
BREAKING: Revolut moved ~2,000 engineers onto self-hosted GLM for coding and pushed Claude Code and Codex to the exception list.
Per David Abitbol, who leads AI ops there: 56 Nvidia B200s, a blended 30 cents per million tokens, roughly a tenth of what they paid Anthropic and OpenAI. Engineering lead time improved 70%.
Here's the part that matters: the gains showed up when tokens stopped being rationed. Engineers quit saving AI for the hard tickets and pointed it at everything.
Frontier models become the exception, open weights become the default. That's a pricing problem for every lab heading to IPO.
h/t @OliverMolander
Would you move your team off frontier APIs if the bill dropped 90%?

articles.title: Netflix will show you themed recommendations through a new ‘AI Discover’ tab
articles.body:
Netflix’s TV app is getting a new “AI Discover” tab where the company will show experimental, AI-powered featuresto help you find new shows and movies to watch.
Netflix will show you themed recommendations through a new ‘AI Discover’ tab
Netflix’s first ‘AI Discover’ feature suggests content based around different themes.
The first of these experiments surfaces content based around themes, like “Something Light,” “Family Movie Night,” or “Quick Watches.” When you pick a theme, Netflix will show you recommendations that match it. If you don’t like a recommendation, you can tell that to Netflix, and the app will remember it.
The company says that AI Discover is powered by “a new intelligence layer we’ve been building that responds to what members tell us in real time and keeps learning.”
AI Discover, which will show up as a “Discover” tab along your top menu, is gradually starting to roll out in the US to “members who use Netflix in English on supported TVs.”
The announcement follows Netflix recently laying off around 1,000 employees as growth has slowed and users are reportedly watching the service less.

articles.title: The Pixel Buds Pro 2 have returned to their lowest price to date
articles.body:
Android owners looking for an earbud upgrade are in luck. The Google Pixel Buds Pro 2 are back down to $169 at Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store, matching the lowest price we’ve seen. Google’s site claims the deal will last until 11:59PM PT on November 8th, and other retailers will likely follow suit. Some colors are already sold out, however, so it’s worth checking multiple retailers if you don’t see your preferred option.
The Pixel Buds Pro 2 have returned to their lowest price to date
You can also grab deals on Fellow’s Aiden coffee maker, an ESR charger, and Borderlands: Game of the Year Edition.
The Pro 2 are great for Android owners and work particularly well with Pixel phones, which receive some extra tricks, including tighter Gemini integration. We praised the wireless earbuds for their improved design, which cut both weight and size while improving the comfort and fit. They have more powerful noise cancellation and a better transparency mode, though they still don’t quite match up to some of the best in the industry, like the latest Bose Ultra Earbuds. The default tuning leans towards clarity and crisp detail, rather than boosted bass, with both presets and a five-band EQ to adjust them to your liking.
Other deals to consider
- Nintendo Switch owners can pick up Borderlands: Game of the Year Edition from the Nintendo Store for just $5.99, a steep discount from the usual price of $29.99. The updated version of the first game in Gearbox’s storied looter-shooter series features “bazillions” of guns, visual upgrades, and all four of the DLC packs. The deal runs until 11:59PM PT on November 6th.
- The refurbished Fellow Aiden is on sale at Fellow’s online storefront for $299.95, a $100 discount. The coffee maker brews anywhere from a single cup to a full carafe of pour-over-quality coffee, with scheduling available both on the machine and via the Aiden app. Refurb units have been thoroughly tested and come with a one-year warranty, too, just in case there are any issues.
- Prime Members can score a 26 percent discount on ESR’s Cyclone Magnetic Charging Pad at Amazon, lowering the price of the silver and black units to $36.99 ($13 off). The wireless charger supports up to 25 watts, with a built-in fan to keep both the charger and your device cool. The integrated stand also lets you use the charger while you catch up on YouTube, and the 5.9-foot cable means you aren’t glued to an outlet.

articles.title: Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027
articles.body:
Meta is planning to release the last OS update for its Quest 2 and Quest Pro VR headsets by March 2027, the company announced today. The last OS update for those devices is planned to be v213, and after that, Meta will continue to ship security patches and critical bug fixes through the end of 2027. Apps that support the Quest 2 or Quest Pro can also be submitted through December 2027, Meta says.
Meta will end Quest 2 OS updates in 2027
The Quest 2 and Pro were discontinued in 2024, and next year, Meta will stop releasing OS updates for the VR headsets.
Meta is calling the Quest 3 and 3S “now the baseline for Meta VR gamers.” The company is announcing this shift ahead of the planned release of its new VR Glasses, which are set to launch sometime in spring 2027.
“Quest 2 and Quest Pro laid the foundation for this platform, and millions of people still play on them,” Meta says. “Quest 3 and Quest 3S give your apps more performance headroom and mixed reality built in, and apps built for them carry forward to Meta VR Glasses, which run on the same OS and SDKs.”
Meta launched the Quest 2 in 2020 and the Quest Pro in 2022. It discontinued both products in 2024.

articles.title: Apple starts giving Siri AI access to third-party apps
articles.body:
Apple will now let Siri AI perform actions across third-party apps. As part of the iOS 27.3 update rolling out on Tuesday, Apple announced developers can now integrate Siri AI’s new features in “all apps,” allowing the voice assistant to draw on a user’s personal context, process natural language prompts, and use on-screen awareness to complete requests.
Apple starts giving Siri AI access to third-party apps
Siri AI will soon be able to carry out tasks across a wider range of apps.
The update, which is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview, also adds a new “app skills” feature that third-party developers can create to combine several tasks into a single action. In Apple’s developer documentation, the company says users won’t have to mention an app’s name in their request while it’s in the foreground, during a Live Activity, or in a conversation with Siri AI about the app.
“For example, a person might request a ride with a ride share app, follow updates to the app’s Live Activity while they wait for their ride to arrive, then request to move the pickup location to a different address by saying ‘Hey Siri, change my ride pickup to a new address,’” Apple says. As noted by 9to5Mac, Apple previously made a smaller set of features available to third-party developers.
Apple is bringing Siri AI’s expanded capabilities to its own apps as well, including Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather apps. “Users can do things like find a coffee shop they visited last week or archive files that haven’t been opened in over a year,” according to Apple. The company notes that users can ask Siri AI what it can do in each app.

As a programming language, ATS is both syntax-rich and feature-rich. This book introduces the reader to some core features of ATS, including basic functional programming, simple types, (recursively defined) datatypes, polymorphic types, dependent types, linear types, theorem-proving, programming with theorem-proving (PwTP), and template-based programming. Although the reader is not assumed to be familiar with programming in general, the book is likely to be rather dense for someone without considerable programming experience.
To Jinning, Zoe, and Chloe.

articles.title: In an Updated Edition, Photographer Ivan McClellan Returns to Black Rodeo Culture
articles.body:
In an Updated Edition, Photographer Ivan McClellan Returns to Black Rodeo Culture
From California to Oklahoma to Illinois, Black communities are saddling up and grasping the reins of a horse or ornery bull. A thriving culture that’s gained attention in recent years, these competitors form bonds in and out of the rodeo arena, where their animals kick up dust and barrel across the ring.
Since 2015, photographer Ivan McClellan has been embedded within these communities across the U.S. His new book, Eight Seconds: Legacy in Motion, is an addendum to his earlier body of work with 91 new images that spotlight the people and places integral to Black rodeo culture.
Published by Damiani, the updated edition features Texan teenager Kortnee Solomon, who’s captivated audiences as one of the youngest competitors, on the cover. Flanked by horses, Solomon stands proudly wearing a rainbow-colored money shirt and blue hat, her eyes shaded by the brim.
Additional images zoom into the arena alongside cowboys racing across the dirt stage and toward the stands, where the audience cheers under the bright, stadium lights. Whereas these industrial bulbs can illuminate journalistic photos of the rodeo in a way that embraces over-exposure, McClellan leans into shadow and a sense of warmth, capturing portraits and candid shots that exude the familiarity and mutual respect of the longstanding relationships he’s built.
Find both the earlier and new edition on Bookshop. Find a larger archive of McClellan’s work on his website and Instagram.

articles.title: SUSE To Cut One In Ten Employees Because of AI
articles.body:
SUSE To Cut One In Ten Employees Because of AI 17
			
		 	
				SUSE plans to cut roughly 10% of its 1,900-person workforce, with CEO Dirk-Peter van Leeuwen saying "automation and AI" are reducing the need for some roles and allowing the open source software company to operate with less overhead and flatter management structures. "We are announcing a reduction of SUSE's global workforce of approximately 10 percent," said Van Leeuwen in an email. "These decisions are painful for our people, our culture, and our open source community, but they are necessary for us to adapt and build a sustainable, resilient SUSE for the long term." The Register reports:  Van Leeuwen says the business, bought by Swedish private equity provider EQT, decided to cut jobs after scrutinizing its "future strategy, required capabilities, and team structures." The rest of the organization will get a look at the fiscal year 2027 strategy on November 16. He said in the message to staff: "What is clear is that automation and AI are fundamentally shifting how software companies operate. AI capabilities are advancing exponentially, forcing us to radically reimagine our work. We have seen this trend already both inside our sector and in the wider economy. This means that the organizational design and cost base that SUSE is built on today will not carry us forward successfully.
"We are adapting. Across SUSE, modern tooling is already changing our daily workflows, enabling teams to move faster with less operational overhead and flatter reporting lines. The requirement for some existing roles has greatly diminished. Other roles will evolve over the next few years. This means we are accelerating investments in high priority areas, and deprioritizing others. These are hard, painful decisions to make, but necessary for our future."
[...] The specific roles at risk of redundancy were not outlined but SUSE claims it has considered where the people in those positions are "able to evolve, what they can stop doing, what they need to do more of - and decisions have been made on that basis." Staff caught up in the redundancies will be informed by November 4, employee representatives nominated the following day, and one to one meetings will begin at the start of next week.  Van Leeuwen says in the internal memo that the job cuts are a "reflection of shifting organizational needs, not your talent or commitment. You have tackled hard infrastructure and open source challenges that power critical enterprise systems around the world. "Any organization will be fortunate to have your expertise."

articles.title: Kalshi and its co-founders face felony charges for violating Utah gambling laws
articles.body:
The Trump administration is trying to stop Utah from enforcing its gambling ban against Kalshi, making Utah the 10th state sued by the US government agency that regulates prediction markets.
Meanwhile, Utah Attorney General Derek Brown filed criminal charges in a state court against Kalshi and its founders on Wednesday. The attorney general’s office provided us with court filings listing charges against KalshiEX, LLC, Kalshi co-founder and CEO Tarek Mansour, and Kalshi co-founder and COO Luana Lopes Lara.
The company and two co-founders each face 13 felony charges and one misdemeanor for violating gambling laws. The charges are based on sports bets offered on Kalshi between September 13 and September 24. “The state did not issue arrest warrants for Monsour and Lopes Lara. Instead, they have been issued summons to respond to the charges in Third District Court in Salt Lake County,” The Salt Lake Tribune wrote.
The Utah News Dispatch quoted a Kalshi statement vowing to fight the charges. “This is a crazy overreach; Utah is clearly playing politics. We look forward to putting a stop to this in court, just like we did in Arizona,” the statement said, referring to similar charges the company beat in Arizona in May.
Utah, which prohibits gambling, filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi in a state court last week. Utah’s lawsuit seeks an order prohibiting Kalshi from offering bets on sports, elections, politics, and other events.
“Kalshi runs an online casino in Utah and calls it a prediction market. That violates Utah law,” Utah Attorney General Derek Brown, a Republican, said last week. “Not only do our state laws ban gambling but Utah is one of only two states where gambling is also prohibited under the state constitution. For 130 years, Utah has been clear: gambling has no place here, and we will enforce our laws.”
Utah already defeated Kalshi in federal court after the prediction market filed a preemptive lawsuit that sought to prevent the state from enforcing its gambling laws. Now that Utah is moving ahead in its attempt to shut down Kalshi, it must defend against a lawsuit filed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

articles.title: OpenAI seems to be silently re-enabling model training on Codex chats
articles.body:
My company is pretty paranoid about leaking IP to the frontier labs through prompts, so we've all been diligent about disabling data sharing in Codex/Claude Code/etc. But yesterday my coworkers and I noticed that the setting had been silently reenabled in Codex. None of us knowingly opted back in.
You can check your settings here: https://chatgpt.com/settings/data-controls. Look for "Improve the model for everyone".
Curious if this is an isolated issue or something more widespread.
EDIT: looks like this has been noted before https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49643556
EDIT: apparently you can also turn off data sharing here: https://privacy.openai.com/policies?modal=take-control

articles.title: Anthropic IPO filing: $1.7B quarterly payroll, about $107K per employee monthly
articles.body:
Winners & losers: It's no secret that if you want some of the most lucrative compensation packages in tech, AI is the industry to be in. That's been perfectly illustrated by Anthropic's amended S-1 filing, which reveals its personnel costs recently averaged over $100,000 per employee per month.
The filing, spotted by Business Insider, shows that Anthropic recorded more than $1.7 billion in personnel expenses from July through to September. With 5,300 people working at the company, that works out at over $322,000 per person over the three-month span, or about $107,300 per employee per month.
Those costs include standard cash salaries along with bonuses, benefits, and employer payroll taxes. The largest share, $1.1 billion, came from Anthropic's stock-based compensation expenses, which reflect the value of company shares employees earn as part of their pay. Anthropic records that value as an expense even though employees don't receive the equivalent amount in cash.
As eye-watering as those figures sound, the wage bill takes up a much smaller slice of Anthropic's revenue than it once did. In 2023, the Claude maker spent more than twice as much on personnel as it brought in from customers. In the first nine months of 2026, personnel costs reached $4.8 billion, or about 15% of the $33.2 billion in revenue Anthropic reported for the same period.
Going public could change things pretty quickly. Anthropic has filed for what could be the biggest IPO ever. Some of its restricted stock units come with two conditions: employees have to work at the company for a certain length of time, and an event such as an IPO has to take place.
Had Anthropic completed its IPO on September 30, 2026, it says it would have recorded an $8.2 billion stock-based compensation charge that day for restricted stock units. That single charge would have exceeded the $4.86 billion Anthropic reported in personnel expenses for the first nine months of 2026. The company expected to recognize another $24.1 billion in expense for those awards over a weighted-average period of about two years, according to its amended filing.
Anthropic has some well-funded competition in the AI business. Last year, OpenAI boss Sam Altman claimed Meta had offered some of his employees $100 million signing bonuses to jump ship. Anthropic has managed to grow its workforce fivefold since the end of 2024, though that still leaves it with fewer than a tenth as many employees as Meta, which has around 67,000 people on its payroll.

articles.title: Apple HomeView Ultra, Drone and Laundry-Folding Robot Reportedly In Development
articles.body:
Apple HomeView Ultra, Drone and Laundry-Folding Robot Reportedly In Development 53
			
		 	
				According to  The Information, Apple is developing a $1,000 HomeView Ultra smart home hub with a 9-inch touchscreen mounted on a motorized arm that can follow users around a room and autonomously respond to its surroundings. It's also said to be experimenting with more ambitious home robots, including a wheeled robot that follows people, a smart home drone and a machine capable of folding laundry. Notebookcheck reports:  According to the report, HomeView Ultra will feature a larger 9-inch touchscreen mounted on a robotic arm. This arm can automatically turn the screen toward the user. With a camera and several sensors, this smart home hub is said to be "fully aware" of its surroundings and capable of acting autonomously. This autonomy ranges from turning on the lights when someone enters the room to shooing a cat away when it jumps onto a table. These sensors are also intended to prevent the arm from hitting nearby objects with the display.
Apple is reportedly currently planning to announce this smart home hub in 2027 for around $1,000, but according to The Information, its launch could be delayed until 2028. The reason is allegedly the software, which has not yet been finalized, while the hardware is said to be ready for market already.

articles.title: The Ford Privacy Promise: You're in Control of Your Data
articles.body:
Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights. With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously. That’s why, today, Ford is announcing the Privacy Promise.
Ford is launching the Privacy Promise to make an explicit commitment to customers that their vehicle data is safe with us and they’re in control of what they share. Our newly launched Privacy Promise website provides education on our privacy practices and how to customize your vehicle data and privacy settings anytime in-vehicle or via the Ford App.
Our Privacy Promise
We know that trust is earned. Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day. Learn about our privacy practices by reading our Privacy Notices.
- Your Privacy Is Our Priority. We design and build our products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use and storage and even disposal. This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect your privacy.
- Straight Talk About Your Data. We strive to provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information. This empowers you to navigate your privacy choices with confidence. Once you make those choices, we respect your decision.
- You Drive Your Privacy Choices. We understand the trust you place in us every time you drive our vehicles and are dedicated to protecting your privacy. We believe using vehicle data to raise the bar on safety and quality is the right thing to do. We offer vehicle privacy settings that allow you to control what data you want to share, subject to the features and services you wish to enjoy. We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers.
Research Insights
As we created the Privacy Promise, Ford wanted to learn more about what customers understood about vehicle and data privacy.
We surveyed just over 1,000 U.S. consumers — both Ford and non-Ford owners. Our customers tell us that vehicle privacy is important to them.
As much as they value privacy, we also learned that customers understand the value of data sharing. A value our survey respondents kept returning to was control: the ability to adjust their settings on demand and in detail.
Ford created the Privacy Promise to help drive awareness of a customer’s responsibility and choices when it comes to their data.
Survey respondents listed automakers as more trusted stewards of privacy than many other large organizations that handle data.
Ford customers, in particular, showed more comfort than non-Ford customers with tech-forward, connected solutions like smart home devices.
How Can I See What Data I Share with Ford?
To learn more about the Privacy Promise, how to customize your vehicle settings, and connected vehicle data, visit our new website.
Kristin Jones is Ford's Chief Privacy Officer and Deputy General Counsel, Data & Privacy.

articles.title: SpaceX Is Reportedly Looking At Buying Boost Mobile
articles.body:
SpaceX Is Reportedly Looking At Buying Boost Mobile (engadget.com) 59
			
		 	
				SpaceX has reportedly held talks with EchoStar about acquiring Boost Mobile or gaining access to its network, potentially giving Starlink a shortcut toward becoming a full-fledged U.S. mobile carrier. Engadget reports:  According to Washington Post's sources, the deal could look like SpaceX acquiring Boost Mobile outright or gaining access to its cell network, which is leased from AT&T and T-Mobile. There could be a major hitch with the deal though, since SpaceX's potential mobile service would need the green light from those major mobile carriers, according to the report. The Washington Post also reported that major cell companies, which include AT&T, T-Mobile and Verizon, have already turned down Musk down for access to its cell networks in order to launch a separate SpaceX service.  Last month, SpaceX reportedly held talks with Crown Castle to access at least 80,000 cellular tower sites across the U.S. as it prepares to launch Starlink Mobile. "We will be building out our terrestrial networks so there's broad-based connectivity anywhere that SpaceX and Starlink are allowed to operate," Musk said during SpaceX's earnings call this week. Satellite launches plus spectrum acquisition "will pave the way for Starlink Mobile to become a major mobile carrier in the US," he said.

articles.title: BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000
articles.body:
BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.
BYD October EV sales reach a record 300,000+
The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.
BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.
To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.
October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.
BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.
According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.
Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.
By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.
Top comment by davesax11
Market is in transition. BYD is dominant, but Geely and others have strong portfolios as well. Legacy manufacturers are slow walking, constrained by habit and unable to make critical strategic decisions in the face of the onslaught.
With several new and updated vehicles launching with its new Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology, BYD aims to continue attracting new buyers with longer range, faster charging, and more tech-oriented models.
Electrek’s Take
While the US is coming off its best quarter of the year in EV sales, BYD’s performance shows how far ahead China is in the transition to electric vehicles.
China continues to lead the global EV market, accounting for over half of all electric cars sold worldwide.
With a wave of low-cost domestic brands flooding China’s market, BYD and other automakers are driving growth overseas in major markets like Europe, South Korea, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America, where legacy OEMs are already falling behind quickly.
